cards.title: Minimum Circuit Size Problem
cards.formal:
Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP), with a complete truth table as input, NP-complete under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time function \(g\) such that
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad x\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g(x)\in\mathrm{MCSP}?\]
Use the exact circuit model and language below. The target is unconditional and unrelativized. A reduction may not use random bits, advice, an oracle, a gap promise, a partial truth table or an implicitly represented truth table.

source_formulation.text: The primary source asks whether ordinary MCSP is NP-hard and separately whether it may be in BPP. The two previously consolidated sources also explicitly ask about NP-hardness. This card takes their common NP-hardness question as its single target and fixes deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial consolidation of the primary source, PDF p.3, with the explicitly shared question in the STACS 2026 and CCC 2023 sources; the separate BPP question remains context

cards.why: MCSP asks how hard it is to recognize computational simplicity from complete data. Its classification connects NP-completeness with circuit lower bounds, learning and cryptography. A proof or refutation of standard NP-hardness would settle a central question about whether circuit minimization has the same reduction-based difficulty as general NP search.
cards.status_note: Source-open: the STACS 2026 introduction explicitly retains ordinary total-MCSP hardness as open. The 2023 primary formulation and gate-model passages, CCC 2023 Theorems 1 and 3/Proposition 2, FOCS 2025 Theorems I.1 and V.7, and the June 2026 ECCC abstract/introduction were checked. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no unconditional deterministic polynomial-time many-one hardness proof or refutation for ordinary MCSP. The 2025 conditional quasipolynomial theorem and 2026 implicit-input preprint do not meet this target. This is a scoped literature check, not independent verification of all cited proofs or exhaustive certification of present openness.

progress.text: The primary source states ordinary MCSP membership in NP and explicitly leaves NP-hardness and efficient randomized algorithms unresolved.
Theorems 1 and 3 give degree and size lower bounds for sum-of-squares refutations of circuit-existence encodings. These are restricted proof-system bounds.
FOCS Theorems I.1 and V.7 prove conditional deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness under all three stated assumptions.
The STACS paper still poses ordinary MCSP hardness and proves that XOR simple extensions can be recognized in polynomial time under both of its gate-count measures.
The ECCC manuscript gives conditional randomized hardness for implicit gap MCSP and explicitly distinguishes ordinary truth-table MCSP.

sentences: The Minimum Circuit Size Problem asks whether a complete Boolean truth table can be computed by a circuit below a given size threshold.
The card fixes AND, OR and NOT gates, counts all gates, and measures input length by the full truth table.
The target is NP-completeness under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions.
Known results for restricted proof systems, conditional quasipolynomial reductions and implicit representations do not settle that target.
A complete answer must prove or refute the existence of a SAT reduction with exactly these guarantees.

context_blocks.text: MCSP asks whether a fully specified Boolean function has a short circuit. Finding a short representation is an optimization task; this decision version asks whether a proposed size threshold can be met. Its input already contains every function value, which makes checking a proposed circuit efficient.

The main target is the NP-hardness question shared by the three source passages consolidated into this card with user approval on 12 September 2026. The original primary passage also raises membership in BPP. That broader classification is retained here as context rather than being silently identified with the negation of NP-hardness.

The circuit basis matters for exact minimization. The 2026 source treats both counting all gates and counting only binary gates; this card explicitly uses its total-gate convention. The source continues to identify ordinary MCSP hardness as open and distinguishes it from successful hardness results for partial specifications.

Austrin and Risse establish strong lower bounds for sum-of-squares refutations of formulas asserting that a small circuit exists. Sum-of-squares is a particular algebraic proof system. Its limitations give information about a restricted method of certifying circuit lower bounds, without proving that every efficient algorithm for ordinary MCSP fails.

Hirahara and Ilango obtain deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness, including constant-factor approximation, under three assumptions together: subexponentially secure noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs for SAT, almost-everywhere subexponential nondeterministic circuit lower bounds for coNP, and almost-everywhere near-maximum circuit lower bounds for \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here nonadaptive means that a reduction prepares all oracle questions before receiving answers. Both its assumptions and its longer running time distinguish this result from the target.

The June 2026 ECCC manuscript studies an implicit version whose function is represented by a circuit sampling labeled examples, rather than by the full table. Its randomized gap-hardness result assumes subexponential versions of indistinguishability obfuscation and the nonexistence of an optimal propositional proof system. This is further progress on a related representation, not an unconditional many-one reduction to the language defined here.

cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an \(n\)-input Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), optional constant sources 0 and 1, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one designated output wire. Wires may feed arbitrarily many gates. An input, a constant or a gate may be the output. The size is the total number of AND, OR and NOT gates; input and constant sources, wires and the output designation are not charged. In particular, NOT gates count. Write \(\operatorname{CC}(f)\) for the minimum such size computing \(f\) on every input. This fixes the total-gate convention, corresponding to the source's \(R\) size measure. It is not the measure that counts only binary gates, nor the basis of all two-input Boolean functions.

The truth table \(t\in\{0,1\}^{N}\), where \(N=2^n\), lists the values of a total function \(f_t:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) in lexicographic input order. A well-formed instance is \((t,s)\), with integer \(0\le s\le N\) written in binary. It is a yes-instance exactly when \(\operatorname{CC}(f_t)\le s\). To fix a binary language, encode a pair as \(1^{|t|}0t\operatorname{bin}(s)\), with no leading zeros in \(\operatorname{bin}(s)\), except that zero is encoded as the single bit 0. Strings failing this syntax, the power-of-two length requirement, \(n\ge1\), or the threshold bound are no-instances. The input length is \(2N+1+O(\log(N+1))\), so polynomial time is measured in the full truth-table length, not merely in the number \(n\) of variables. The redundant unary length prefix is only a fixed efficiently decodable pair encoding.

Constants have been made explicit to remove a convention left implicit in the source. For a nonconstant function, constant inputs can be eliminated gate by gate without increasing size, so allowing them does not change its optimum. For the two constant functions the answer follows directly from the specified convention. No claim that all Boolean bases preserve exact optimum sizes is needed.

A deterministic polynomial-time function is computed by one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts on every input of length \(m\) within \(C(m+1)^d\) steps, for some constants \(C,d\). It has no advice or oracle. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(L\) to \(K\) is such a function \(g\) satisfying \(x\in L\) if and only if \(g(x)\in K\) for every binary string \(x\). Its output is one ordinary instance, whose entire description is written within that time bound. SAT is satisfiability of finite Boolean formulas over AND, OR and NOT in a fixed explicit binary syntax; malformed formulas are no-instances. Any two usual efficiently interconvertible formula encodings give the same reduction question.

NP consists of languages for which a yes-instance has a certificate of polynomial length that a uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine verifies, with no certificate accepted on a no-instance. A language is NP-hard here if every language in NP reduces to it by the specified many-one reductions, and NP-complete if it is also in NP. MCSP is in NP: a circuit with at most \(s\le N\) gates has an explicit topologically ordered description of \(O(N\log(N+1))\) bits, and evaluating it on all \(N\) assignments checks the entire table in polynomial time. Thus the displayed SAT reduction suffices, by SAT's NP-completeness, and its nonexistence would refute NP-completeness under this reduction convention.

For context only, P denotes uniform deterministic polynomial time and BPP uniform randomized polynomial time with worst-case polynomial running time and error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The source also asks whether MCSP might lie in BPP. That is a separate proposition, not the logical negation of NP-hardness: the two possibilities are not an unconditional exhaustive or disjoint classification.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the displayed SAT-to-MCSP reduction. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic reduction, prove its polynomial running time and output length, and prove the yes/no equivalence for every input using the exact total truth-table and gate-count conventions above. A negative answer must prove that every deterministic polynomial-time candidate reduction fails on some input. A conditional theorem, an oracle-relative theorem, hardness under randomized or quasipolynomial-time reductions, a lower bound for a restricted proof system, or hardness of a partial, implicit or gap variant does not alone meet this criterion. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this exact language-reduction statement.

cards.title: NL versus UL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist one nondeterministic Turing machine \(M\) and constants \(C,D,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, on every explicitly encoded directed-reachability input \(x=(G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), every computation branch halts within \(D(N+2)^k\) steps and visits at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells, and
\[\#\{\text{accepting computation branches of }M(x)\}=
\begin{cases}1,&t\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }G,\\0,&\text{otherwise}?\end{cases}\]
The constants and machine are independent of the input. Unreachable and malformed inputs must have no accepting branch.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Use a self-delimiting explicit binary list of all vertices and all directed edges, together with \(s,t\in[n]\). In particular, isolated vertices are represented and \(N\ge n\); a binary vertex count is not a succinct description of an exponentially large graph. Edges are ordered pairs of vertices. Self-loops are allowed, and repeated edge entries may be interpreted as the same edge. A directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) follows the listed edge directions, and the length-zero path is allowed when \(s=t\). No planarity, acyclicity, bounded-degree or unique-path promise is present. Invalid list structure or out-of-range vertices make the encoding malformed. Validity is deterministically checkable in logarithmic space, by rescanning the input if needed. Explicit adjacency lists, edge lists and adjacency matrices are interchangeable here through deterministic logarithmic-space reductions of polynomial output length.

The machine has a finite description with a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over finite alphabets. Heads use ordinary Turing-machine moves. The space bound counts all distinct work-tape cells visited on a branch, including blank cells crossed, counters and every temporary record. Input cells and finite control do not count. The output is acceptance or rejection. No advice, randomness, oracle, writable input, catalytic tape or other uncharged storage is available. Every branch, including a rejecting branch, obeys the same polynomial clock and logarithmic-space bounds.

A computation branch is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to halting. Two sequences that merge into the same configuration still count as distinct branches. The condition counts successful computations, not distinct accepting configurations, output values, graph paths or certificates after identifying equivalent strings. Rejecting branches need not be unique. The machine is not required to output the graph path or to behave deterministically.

For languages of binary strings, \(\mathrm{NL}\) is acceptance by nondeterministic machines under these time and space bounds, allowing any positive number of accepting branches on a yes input and none on a no input. The subclass \(\mathrm{UL}\) requires at most one accepting branch on every input, hence exactly one on a yes input. A polynomial all-branch clock is the usual equivalent convention for logarithmic-space acceptance. The class equality quantifies separately over languages and machines: every language in NL must have some UL machine. It does not additionally require an effective compiler mapping descriptions of arbitrary NL machines to UL machines.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such reductions preserve the answer and can be composed with a UL machine by deterministically recomputing required output bits; this does not add accepting branches. Its membership in UL therefore implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\); the reverse inclusion follows from the definitions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) for the specified uniform model. An affirmative reachability construction must supply one machine and fixed constants and establish its exact accepting-branch count, correctness on all inputs, and every-branch time and space bounds. A negative answer must prove that some NL language is outside UL, equivalently exclude every proposed reachability machine with these guarantees; the class/reachability equivalence must be justified if used. The graph itself may have arbitrarily many paths, so a promise of a unique graph path cannot replace the required algorithmic unambiguity. A larger-space simulation, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, an oracle, an unproved hardness assumption or a lower bound only for a restricted isolation procedure does not settle the exact question. No approximate branch count or resource estimate is accepted.
cards.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

importance.reason: A basic class equality tying directed reachability, isolation, pseudorandomness and the structure of low-memory witnesses.

progress.text: Reinhardt–Allender show that min-isolation supports unambiguous reachability and prove the nonuniform equality NL/poly=UL/poly.
Van Melkebeek–Prakriya obtain a polynomial-time unambiguous simulation using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space; CCC 2017 and SICOMP 2019.
Doron–Pyne–Tell–Williams derive linear-space unambiguity from substantially weakened but still unproved uniform circuit lower bounds.
The v3 catalytic result places reachability in polynomial time with logarithmic ordinary workspace, \(O((\log N)^2)\) restorable catalytic bits and UL oracle access.
The Pyne–Tell survey distinguishes the conditional logspace equality from the refined conditional linear-space simulation in Theorems 3.12–3.13.
Hoza proves that deterministic oblivious min-isolation for all layered digraphs requires quasipolynomial-size weights in the general parameter regime.
Dinesh and Sasidharan establish UL ∩ coUL algorithms for recognizing simple path graphs and deciding their reachability; the result retains this structural restriction.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic computation may have many successful branches. Unambiguity permits extensive guessing and arbitrarily many rejecting branches, but requires only one successful branch on each yes input. The restriction is on computations of the algorithm, not on the number of paths that happen to exist in the input graph.

The inclusions \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) explain the stakes. An equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) would not by itself remove nondeterminism. A separation would also imply \(\mathrm{L}\ne\mathrm{NL}\). Requiring every reachable machine configuration to have a unique path from the start is a stronger condition, called reach unambiguity, and is not imposed here.

Reinhardt and Allender’s theorem connects unambiguous reachability with min-isolation: positive integer edge weights are min-isolating when every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. With polynomially bounded weights that are available in deterministic logarithmic space, this condition supports logarithmic-space unambiguous reachability. Existence of suitable weights alone does not guarantee that a uniform small-space machine can obtain them.

Their nonuniform result is \(\mathrm{NL}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{UL}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here an advice string of polynomial length may depend on the input length and be shared by all inputs of that length, with no efficient procedure required to generate it. Ordinary UL has no such advice.

Van Melkebeek and Prakriya prove that every NL language has an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation using \(O((\log N)^{3/2})\) workspace. This is an unconditional simulation for all inputs, but the extra square-root-of-logarithm factor is unbounded and prevents this theorem from establishing membership in UL.

The 2025 hardness-based result concerns the scaled-up inclusion \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\mathrm{USPACE}[O(n)]\): these classes use linear nondeterministic and unambiguous workspace. Its hypothesis is a circuit lower bound with specified uniformity and unambiguous-space oracle access. The 2026 survey’s Theorems 3.12 and 3.13 distinguish an older conditional logspace equality from the refined conditional linear-space theorem. Neither is an unconditional resolution.

The February 2026 catalytic result permits \(O((\log N)^2)\) additional writable bits initially containing arbitrary data, whose contents must be restored, as well as a UL oracle. It keeps ordinary workspace logarithmic and time polynomial. Both the extra restorable tape and the oracle are absent from the machine model in this card.

Hoza’s July 2026 theorem concerns a single weight function chosen without inspecting which edges are present. If it must min-isolate every layered graph of width \(w\ge2\) and length \(\ell\ge2\), the maximum weight must be at least \(2^{\Omega(\log w\log\ell)}\). Layered means there are \(\ell+1\) successive layers of \(w\) vertices each, with edges only to the next layer. This excludes polynomially bounded universal weights in the general regime, but does not exclude graph-dependent weights or arbitrary unambiguous algorithms.

The August 2026 MFCS paper gives unambiguous and co-unambiguous logarithmic-space algorithms for recognizing simple path graphs and for their reachability problem. Such a graph has at most one simple path from the specified start to each vertex; directed cycles are still permitted. Recognition is part of the result, but the graph restriction remains essential.

Hoza’s July 2026 theorem concerns a single weight function chosen without inspecting which edges are present. If it must min-isolate every layered graph of width \(w\ge2\) and length \(\ell\ge2\), the maximum weight must be at least \(2^{\Omega(\log w\log\ell)}\). Layered means there are \(\ell+1\) successive layers of \(w\) vertices each, with edges only to the next layer. This excludes polynomially bounded universal weights in the general regime, but does not exclude graph-dependent weights or arbitrary unambiguous algorithms.

The August 2026 MFCS paper gives unambiguous and co-unambiguous logarithmic-space algorithms for recognizing simple path graphs and for their reachability problem. Such a graph has at most one simple path from the specified start to each vertex; directed cycles are still permitted. Recognition is part of the result, but the graph restriction remains essential.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and a constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), directed graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(s,t\in[n]\), the machine halts, correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and visits at most
\[C\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\]
work-tape cells? The graph is given explicitly by its adjacency matrix; the input is read-only. The machine and constant must work for all input sizes.
cards.definitions:
A directed graph has a set \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) of ordered edges. Self-loops are allowed. Reachability asks whether there are vertices \(v_0=s,\ldots,v_\ell=t\), with \(\ell\ge0\), such that \((v_{i-1},v_i)\in E\) for every \(1\le i\le\ell\). In particular \(s=t\) is a yes instance. No degree, planarity, acyclicity or unique-path restriction is imposed.

The input contains a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\), all \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, and \(s,t\) in fixed-length binary vertex fields. Its bit length is \(N=\Theta(n^2)\), so logarithmic bounds in \(N+2\) and \(n+2\) agree up to constants. Malformed strings, including invalid dimensions and vertex fields, are rejected with logarithmic workspace in their actual length. A validity check does not need to store the matrix. The representation is an explicit string, not an adjacency oracle or a circuit describing a much larger graph.

The computation uses a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Heads move by ordinary Turing-machine steps. Space is the total number of distinct work-tape cells visited during the computation, including blank cells crossed by heads, all counters, stacks and auxiliary records. The finite control and read-only input cells are uncharged. There is no advice depending on input size, oracle, random tape, external storage, writable input or extra tape whose contents can temporarily be borrowed. The output is a single accept/reject decision. Input rescanning and arbitrary finite computation are permitted, but every input must eventually halt.

The class \(\mathrm{L}\) consists of languages of binary strings decided by such deterministic machines using \(O(\log(N+2))\) space. The class \(\mathrm{NL}\) uses a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation with the same space bound: an input is accepted exactly when at least one computation branch accepts. One may require a polynomial clock on every branch without changing NL. A logarithmic-space configuration has only polynomially many possibilities, including input-head positions; any accepting computation can therefore be shortened and a logarithmic-size clock suffices. A halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine automatically runs in polynomial time because a repeated complete configuration would repeat forever.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such a reduction writes one polynomial-length instance and preserves its yes/no answer while using logarithmic workspace; output bits can be recomputed when composing it with another small-space machine. Thus a positive answer for the specified matrix representation implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{L}\), and \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) already holds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\), using the stated uniform machine model. An affirmative reachability solution must specify one machine and a constant, and prove correctness, termination, malformed-input handling and the space bound on every input. A negative solution must exclude every such machine: equivalently, for every always-halting correct deterministic reachability decider and every constant \(C\), some valid instance exceeds \(C\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) visited work cells. A class-based argument must establish the equivalence to this concrete reachability target. A lower bound for one search procedure, or a successful algorithm restricted to undirected graphs, using advice, nondeterminism or a higher power of logarithmic space, is insufficient. No numerical approximation of a resource bound answers this exact class-equality question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams give two fixed algorithms with a per-graph guarantee: at least one succeeds, either solving directed reachability in deterministic polynomial time and polylogarithmic space, or estimating length-n random-walk probabilities in nondeterministic logarithmic space. Both report failure and always respect their resource bounds. This alternative does not provide a deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm on all graphs.

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary graph search can remember which vertices have been visited. Logarithmic space holds only a constant number of vertex names and counters, so a separate visited bit for each vertex does not fit. Repeated scans of the input are free of a space penalty, but any saved information between scans counts.

Directed reachability captures an entire complexity class because a small-space machine has only polynomially many configurations. Its legal next steps form the edges of a directed graph, and acceptance is reachability of an accepting configuration. This correspondence is computable with logarithmic workspace.

Savitch’s theorem gives deterministic reachability using \(O((\log n)^2)\) workspace, with a quasipolynomial time bound. The gap between one and two logarithmic factors is exactly relevant to membership in L: an always-halting deterministic machine using only logarithmic space has polynomially many configurations, and hence polynomial running time.

Reingold’s theorem meets the logarithmic-space target when edges are undirected. Directed graphs therefore cannot be replaced by their undirected versions: forgetting an arrow can create paths absent from the original instance.

The equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) means that nondeterministic logarithmic space can recognize both reachability and nonreachability. It is a closure theorem within the nondeterministic model, and does not establish that either task has a deterministic logarithmic-space algorithm.

The 2025 alternative links graph connectivity to random-walk estimation, but its successful procedure may differ from graph to graph. Its deterministic branch uses polylogarithmic rather than logarithmic space. Neither qualification disappears merely because both algorithms signal their own failures.

The 2026 hardness result locates the difficulty even in graphs whose edges split into two sets, each a collection of directed paths of length at most two. This remains NL-hard when the decomposition is part of the input. The pieces are simple, but paths using edges from both pieces can still express general directed reachability.

cards.title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
cards.formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.

source_formulation.text: The search for a complete problem in TFNP is of primary concern to certain fields such as cryptography, but it remains open whether such a […]

cards.why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.

sentences: TFNP contains search problems with polynomially bounded, efficiently verifiable answers guaranteed to exist for every binary input.
The question asks whether one problem in this class is complete for all the others under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions.
Each reduction makes one transformed instance and must decode every valid returned answer correctly.
The complete relation is fixed universally, while the reduction and its polynomial bounds may vary with the source problem.
Known subclass completeness and oracle results clarify the structure without settling this general existence question.

cards.definitions:
Let \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), let \(\Sigma^*\) include the empty string, and let \(|x|\) be bit length. A search relation is a subset \(R\subseteq\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\). An answer to input \(x\) is any string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); no uniqueness or ordering of valid answers is required.

The relation belongs to \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) if all three conditions hold. First, there are positive integers \(a,b\), fixed for \(R\), such that every valid pair satisfies \(|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\). Second, a deterministic algorithm decides \(R(x,y)\) in time at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\), for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Third,
\[\forall x\in\Sigma^*\ \exists y\in\Sigma^*,\qquad R(x,y).\]
Thus totality applies to every binary input. A relation based on a structured encoding must also prescribe a valid answer for malformed instances; restricting the domain to inputs promised to have a solution is insufficient. The output bound is part of the relation: an overlong string is not a valid answer.

Algorithms use uniform finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machines over fixed finite alphabets, with binary input and output. Time counts bit operations, input handling and writing the output, in the worst case over all inputs. A pair can be encoded as \(\langle x,z\rangle=1^{|x|}0xz\), whose length is linear in \(|x|+|z|+1\); malformed encodings may be assigned an arbitrary fixed output. All functions used below are total and polynomial-time computable on their full encoded domains. There is no randomness, advice, nonuniform circuit family or external oracle available to these functions.

For \(R,Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\), the reduction \(R\le_m^p Q\) means that there are functions \(f:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) and \(g:\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) computed in deterministic polynomial time such that
\[\forall x,z\in\Sigma^*,\qquad Q(f(x),z)\ \Longrightarrow\ R(x,g(x,z)).\]
The bound for \(f\) is polynomial in \(|x|\), and that for \(g\) is polynomial in \(|x|+|z|\). The decoder may use the original input \(x\). This is a single transformed instance with a single returned answer; correctness must hold for every possible valid answer, without controlling which answer is returned. The reduction does not itself compute an answer to \(Q\), and the quantification over valid answers is not an oracle supplied to \(f\) or \(g\). Multiple adaptive instance queries are not the reduction in this question.

The complete problem \(Q\), its verifier and its balance bound are fixed before \(R\) is chosen. The reduction functions and their polynomial constants may depend on \(R\) and \(Q\), but not on the particular input. No single effective procedure that recognizes TFNP membership or produces reductions from arbitrary verifier descriptions is required.

A negative answer is the exact opposite quantifier statement:
\[\forall Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \exists R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\not\le_m^p Q.\]
The target is completeness for a search class under the specified search reduction. Completeness of a decision language, completeness for a proper TFNP subclass, or an NP search problem that lacks answers on some inputs does not by itself satisfy it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify one relation \(Q\), prove its polynomial balance, deterministic polynomial-time verifiability and totality on all binary inputs, and establish the stated reductions from every \(R\in\mathrm{TFNP}\). A negative answer must prove that every candidate \(Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\) fails to receive such a reduction from some relation in the class. No effective enumeration of all TFNP problems is additionally required. A subclass-completeness result, a separation relative to an oracle or a conditional consequence alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source states nonexistence of a many-one complete TFNP problem among the central conjectures connecting computational complexity and proof systems. This card asks the equivalent yes-or-no existence question, so the commonly stated conjecture predicts a negative answer.

Polynomial verifiability and a polynomial answer bound can be given by machine descriptions, but totality asserts a condition over all inputs. This semantic requirement prevents simply treating every polynomial-time verifier as a total search problem. Pudlák relates the general completeness question to the ability of fixed arithmetical theories to capture total search, and proves a universal-problem result for suitable classes whose totality is provable in a fixed theory.

Many important subclasses have complete problems tied to particular existence principles. The December 2025 manuscript studies further oracle hierarchies and collapses within TFNP; these subclass results do not supply a complete problem for the entire class.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.

cards.title: Ruling out quasilinear-time SAT without a space restriction
cards.formal:
Is Boolean-formula satisfiability outside deterministic quasilinear time, with no independent bound on the algorithm’s working memory? In the uniform random-access model below, the exact target is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\right],\]
where \(N\) is the full bit length of the explicitly written formula and \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. Thus every fixed polynomial-logarithmic factor must be excluded. On 16 September 2026 the user selected this meaning of the source’s “near-linear time”; the stronger exclusion of all \(N^{1+o(1)}\)-time algorithms is not required.
cards.why: An unconditional time-only lower bound for SAT in a general random-access model would cross a fundamental barrier in complexity theory. Even this comparatively weak exclusion remains separate from the substantial lower bounds known when memory is restricted.
cards.status_note: Source-open under the user-selected n·polylog(n) interpretation without an independent space restriction. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no unconditional matching time-only resolution. cards.definitions:
A Boolean formula is a finite explicitly written expression built from Boolean variables, constants 0 and 1, binary AND and OR, and unary NOT. Its parse structure is a tree; repeated subexpressions are written separately. Variable occurrences use binary identifiers in \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers allowed. Fix a self-delimiting prefix encoding with gate tokens and delimited identifiers. The total bit length \(N\) includes the parse structure and every identifier occurrence. SAT consists of the well-formed encodings for which some assignment to the occurring variables makes the formula evaluate to 1. All malformed strings are rejected. This is decision, not counting assignments or outputting one. Inputs are arbitrary explicit strings, not succinct circuits describing exponentially long formulas.

Fix a uniform deterministic word-RAM with logarithmic-size words. A machine is one finite program independent of \(N\), together with a fixed integer \(b\ge1\) giving word length \(w_N=b\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). It has a fixed number of word registers and an initially zero writable memory array addressed by \(w_N\)-bit integers. The input is separately read-only, packed into words with zero padding in its final word, and its bit length is available. One step is a register copy, Boolean bitwise operation, addition or subtraction modulo \(2^{w_N}\), comparison, conditional branch, shift by a register-specified count, or indexed read/write of one word. Shifts by at least \(w_N\) return zero. Registers and memory words contain exactly \(w_N\) bits; no unbounded-integer operation has unit cost. The program has no advice, oracle, nondeterminism or random bits. It halts with a single accept/reject answer on every input. Standard additional arithmetic operations on logarithmic words can be implemented with polynomial-logarithmic overhead and do not change the union of time bounds in this question.

There is no logarithmic, sublinear or other independent workspace requirement. The algorithm may use any addressable working memory it can access during its allowed running time. Initial memory is zero, not an input-dependent precomputed table; reading and writing memory are charged. The word-size/address convention is the ordinary polynomial-address-space convention of this RAM model, not a small-space promise. In particular, maintaining an input-sized array is allowed. The purpose of random access is to charge actual computation rather than the distance a sequential input head must travel.

For a fixed \(k\), membership in the displayed time class means that some one machine and constant \(D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) correctly decide every input \(x\) within
\[D(N+2)\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\]
steps, including parsing and rejection of malformed inputs. Here \(k,D,b\) and the finite program are independent of the particular input and its length. The target’s positive statement excludes every such choice. Its negative statement requires just one correct algorithm and one fixed exponent \(k\); it does not require a linear-time algorithm.

The chosen bound is \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\), the union over all fixed logarithmic powers. It is smaller than the broader \(N^{1+o(1)}\) family: for example, \(N2^{\sqrt{\log_2 N}}\) is in the latter family but exceeds \(N(\log N)^k\) for every fixed \(k\). Excluding every \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\) algorithm does not require proving a fixed exponent lower bound \(N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The user-approved clarification retains the absence of a memory restriction and records which of these meanings is being benchmarked.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed time-only nonmembership statement for the stated uniform machine and input model. A positive answer must exclude all fixed \(k,D,b\) and all correct total programs, with no extra workspace restriction. Equivalently, for every correct total program, every \(k\), and every \(D\), some input exceeds its proposed quasilinear bound. A negative answer must provide one program and fixed constants and prove correctness and that time bound on all inputs. A lower bound only for logarithmic-memory algorithms, a restricted SAT-solver family, a particular input distribution, or a sequential-access model does not establish this RAM target. A conditional lower bound under P ≠ NP or an exponential-time hypothesis is not an unconditional solution. Exact asymptotic quantifiers apply; no finite timing experiment or numerical error tolerance settles the question.

context_blocks.text: P versus NP asks whether SAT admits any polynomial-time algorithm. This card asks for a much smaller first exclusion: algorithms only a fixed logarithmic factor slower than reading the input. Such an exclusion would still be consistent with a quadratic or higher-degree polynomial-time SAT algorithm.

Checking a supplied assignment is easy relative to the size of an explicit formula, but this does not show that deciding whether an assignment exists must take longer. The target requires an unconditional separation between existence testing and this very fast deterministic computation, over all possible programs.

Known time-space bounds exclude algorithms that are simultaneously fast and use little writable memory. Williams’s theorem reaches a polynomial time exponent below 2 cos(π/7) when workspace is subpolynomial. Here memory is unrestricted, so that qualification cannot be dropped.

The 2016 column also describes an either/or theorem: SAT cannot have both a quasilinear-time algorithm and a logarithmic-space algorithm, even if these are different algorithms. An either/or conclusion does not identify the time alternative as the true one. It therefore leaves this time-only target unresolved.

Hirahara, Lu and Ren’s 2023 Remark 47 explicitly separates simultaneous time-space bounds from separate-algorithm alternatives. Their discussion still allows the unresolved possibility of quasilinear-time SAT together with polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth parallel circuits. That discussion supplies no quasilinear SAT algorithm and no time-only lower bound.

The source uses “near-linear” informally. The selected meaning excludes every fixed logarithmic power, including arbitrarily large fixed ones. This gives a definite success condition without demanding the stronger exclusion of every subpolynomial overhead or a particular positive power improvement. The selection was made explicitly by the user.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do constants \(a,b,c>0\) and \(q\ge 1\) exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a \(\log _{2}(N+2)\) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most \((N+2)^{b}\) symbols over an alphabet of size at most \((N+2)^{b}\), with perfect completeness and soundness at most \((N+2)^{- c}\)?
cards.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with \(O(\log  N)\) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most \((N+2)^{- c}\). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.

cards.why: A central quantitative PCP barrier controlling the strength of gap amplification and inapproximability.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{P}_{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{R}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) for the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered field of real numbers?
cards.definitions: Inputs are finite tuples \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. It can store and copy real numbers, perform +, −, ×, and division by a nonzero number, and branch on the sign or equality to zero of a stored real, at unit cost per operation; the ordinary BSS input, output and register-shift operations are included. \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of subsets of the disjoint union of the spaces \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\) decidable by one such deterministic machine in polynomially many steps as a function of n. \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb{R}}\) consists of sets for which membership of x is equivalent to existence of a real witness y of length bounded by a polynomial in n that is accepted by one deterministic BSS verifier in polynomially many steps. Machine constants are finite and independent of input length; witnesses may contain arbitrary reals. The target is equality of these classes, not equality in a finite-precision or bit-cost model.

context_blocks.text: The BSS model treats exact field operations and order tests as elementary computation. Its version of nondeterminism allows real witnesses and captures basic real algebraic feasibility problems.

This separation is a foundational question about algebraic computation over a continuum. Classical P versus NP does not by itself answer it: the input representation, cost model and certificates differ.

The recommended paper studies Boolean inputs to real computation. Proposition 1.1 identifies \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\), where the superscript 0 permits only machine constants 0 and 1. PosSLP asks whether an arithmetic straight-line program using 0, 1, addition, subtraction and multiplication outputs a positive integer. Theorem 1.4 places PosSLP in the counting hierarchy.

With arbitrary fixed real constants, \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R})\) is Conjecture 1.2 in that paper. These Boolean-input results do not settle equality of deterministic and nondeterministic BSS classes on arbitrary real inputs.

cards.title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\exists\mathbb{R}=\mathrm{NP}\) under polynomial-time many-one reductions between finitely encoded decision problems?
cards.definitions: Let ETR be the following language of finite binary strings. An instance is an existential sentence \(\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), where \(\Phi\) is an explicitly represented Boolean formula with atoms \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Each \(p\) is an integer-coefficient polynomial, supplied as a list of monomials with coefficients and nonnegative exponents in binary. Parentheses, connectives, variable indices and all lengths are explicitly encoded; invalid encodings are rejected. Truth uses exact real arithmetic as mathematical semantics, not unit-cost computation. \(\exists\mathbb R\) is the class of languages reducible to ETR by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in input bit length. \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with polynomial-length binary witnesses checked by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. Equivalent fixed finite-tape machine conventions may be used. The question is unrelativized.

Relativized structural results do not decide whether ordinary finite binary certificates suffice for the unrelativized class.

cards.title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
cards.formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
cards.why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.

The proposal asks whether some polynomial-size DNFs require superpolynomial-size deterministic decomposable circuits for the same Boolean function.
Determinism requires disjoint alternatives, while decomposability requires conjunctions to separate their variables.
A separation would show that imposing these useful structural restrictions can force an inherent representation-size increase.

The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

cards.definitions: Inputs are Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). A DNF is a finite disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of distinct literals with no contradictory pair; the empty conjunction is true and the empty disjunction false. Its size is one plus its number of terms and literal occurrences. An NNF circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, leaves labeled by literals or the constants zero and one, and internal AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in. It may share subcircuits and have unrestricted depth. Its size is its total number of vertices and edges. The variable set of a gate comprises variables labeling leaves that reach it. Decomposability means that the variable sets of different children of every AND gate are pairwise disjoint. Determinism means that, for every OR gate and every assignment to the union of its children’s variable sets, at most one child evaluates to one. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions. Equivalent circuits agree for every input assignment, with no error or auxiliary existentially quantified variables. There is no common variable order, tree-structured decomposition, restriction to decision gates, or uniformity requirement. Polynomial comparisons use the DNF representation size, including all literal occurrences; ordinary explicit gate/edge encodings give the same polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction. The family formulation using polynomial-size DNFs in the number of inputs is equivalent after permitting unused input variables as padding.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability separates the variable sets of conjunctions, while determinism makes the alternatives at each disjunction disjoint. These restrictions support exact model counting in time polynomial in the representation size. A DNF already satisfies decomposability after inconsistent terms are removed, but its terms need not be disjoint.

Capelli’s June 2026 habilitation explicitly asks for a superpolynomial d-DNNF lower bound for DNF formulas. The known separation of unrestricted DNNF from d-DNNF uses a broader source representation and therefore does not settle this DNF restriction.

Even if every DNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representation, finding one in polynomial time would have additional counting consequences. The source distinguishes this algorithmic conversion issue from the existence of small representations; conditional conversion hardness supplies no unconditional size separation.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified superpolynomial size separation, or refute it by proving that one polynomial bounds the minimum equivalent d-DNNF size for every DNF. A negative answer need not give an efficient converter. A lower bound for decision-DNNF, structured d-DNNF, or a broader DNNF input family does not meet the stated unrestricted-output, DNF-input criterion.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(\mathrm{P}(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\); no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.

context_blocks.text: CLS captures total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani proved that it equals PPAD∩PLS, connecting this optimization class to two discrete existence principles.

The equivalent task presented here gives two independent succinct problems and asks for a solution to either one. The known completeness theorem means that an efficient algorithm for this task would solve every problem in CLS. The theorem identifies the class; it does not supply a polynomial-time solution algorithm.

Solving both component instances is not required. A restricted-circuit algorithm, a randomized algorithm alone, or a conditional hardness implication does not establish either unconditional answer to \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\).

cards.title: Polynomial-size circuits for EXP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), decidable by one deterministic exponential-time algorithm, whose circuit complexity \(s_L(n)\) satisfies \[\forall C\geq1\;\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\forall N\geq1\;\exists n\geq N:\quad s_L(n)>C(n+1)^{k}?\]
cards.why: This is a central test of whether explicit computation can be proved to require large unrestricted Boolean circuits. Resolving it would cross the gap between uniform time hierarchy theorems and lower bounds that defeat arbitrary nonuniform circuit families.

cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\geq1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{a}})\), with the usual multiplicative constants and polynomially equivalent deterministic multitape Turing-machine encodings. The input is an arbitrary binary string and the machine decides membership without a promise, advice or oracle. A Boolean circuit on \(n\) inputs is an acyclic graph using fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, constants, and one output. Its size is the number of noninput gates; replacing this by its explicit gate-and-wire encoding length preserves polynomial size. The quantity \(s_L(n)\) is the minimum such size for exact agreement with membership in \(L\) on all \(n\)-bit strings. Circuit choices for different lengths are arbitrary and need not be computable. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) comprises languages with \(s_L(n)\leq C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\) depending on the language. The quantifiers in the question require one language defeating every polynomial size bound; they do not require a lower bound at every sufficiently large length. The source uses exponential-time notation in a truth-table generation discussion; the card uses the standard union defining EXP. Using \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\) instead gives the equivalent class-containment question by polynomial padding.

context_blocks.text: The deterministic time hierarchy separates polynomial from exponential uniform running time. It does not rule out small circuits chosen independently at each input length, which is the nonuniform issue in this conjecture.

Wigderson states the separation as Conjecture 8.6 in a discussion of explicit hard Boolean functions and pseudorandomness. Counting shows that many truth tables need large circuits, but the conjecture additionally places a hard language in a fixed uniform exponential-time class.

A 2026 preprint by Atserias and Müller proves a consistency result relating bounded arithmetic to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Consistency of the separation with a formal theory is distinct from a proof of the separation itself.

The public note proposes a weaker upper-bound question: whether every EXP language has subexponential-size circuits. For example, one precise convention is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{EXP}\;\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N:\ s_L(n)\le 2^{\varepsilon n}\). Polynomial-size circuits would imply this upper bound. It is consequently weaker than the containment \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), which is the negative answer to the present separation question, rather than a weaker form of the conjectured lower bound. The displayed convention specifies this contextual variant; it is not substituted for the card’s original target.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\), including an EXP language and the quantified superpolynomial lower bound, or prove its negation \(\mathrm{EXP}\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Different hard languages for different fixed exponents, a lower bound for a restricted gate basis, or a consistency theorem alone do not settle the question.

cards.title: Exponential depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) lower bounds for E
cards.formal:
Does there exist a language \(L\in\mathrm E\) whose characteristic functions require exponential-size depth-at-most-three Boolean AND/OR circuits, with arbitrary fan-in and input negations, at infinitely many input lengths?

Let \(f_{L,n}(x)=1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), and let \(S_3(f)\) be the minimum number of AND/OR gates in such a circuit computing \(f\) exactly. The question is
\[\exists L\in\mathrm E\ \exists\delta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad S_3(f_{L,n})>2^{\delta n}.\]
Here \(N,n\) are integers. This makes the source’s class lower-bound target precise as failure of subexponential-size depth-three computation for one language in E. No almost-every-length strengthening is imposed.

sentences: The question asks for one language decidable in deterministic time exponential in input length but requiring exponential-size depth-three Boolean circuits.

A fixed positive lower-bound exponent must hold at infinitely many lengths for the same E language.

cards.definitions:
The class \(\mathrm E\) consists of languages \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) for which there are one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and a fixed positive integer \(c\) such that, on every binary string \(x\) of length \(n\), the machine halts within \(2^{c(n+1)}\) steps and outputs the membership bit of \(L\). The machine uses fixed finite alphabets, and time counts tape operations, input handling and output. There is no advice, oracle, randomness or promise restricting inputs. No separate space bound is imposed. The same \(M,c\) work at every length. This distinguishes E from unrestricted exponential time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\) and from exponential-time computation with an NP oracle.

A circuit for an \(n\)-input function is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Its sources are constants \(0,1\) and literals \(x_i,\neg x_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\). Each internal gate is AND or OR of a nonempty finite list of predecessor values. Fan-in and fan-out have no fixed bound; computed values may be shared. A gate may also have a single predecessor. An output may be a literal or constant. The circuit must agree with the function on every assignment to all \(n\) variables.

Depth is the largest number of internal AND/OR gates on a source-to-output path and is at most three. Input negations do not contribute to depth; there are no internal NOT, parity, modular-counting, threshold or arbitrary truth-table gates. The size is the number of internal AND/OR gates, counting a shared gate once. Constants, literal sources and wires are not separately charged. The minimum over this class is \(S_3(f)\), which is defined for every Boolean function because a disjunctive normal form is available. Constant and literal outputs have size zero. Both possible top-gate orientations, including OR–AND–OR and AND–OR–AND, are allowed; the lower bound must cover the entire stated class.

All bottom gates have unrestricted fan-in. Neither the function nor the circuit is required to be monotone: a circuit can use both polarities of every variable. Although the notation refers to the depth-three AC-zero gate model, candidate circuits here are allowed exponential size; a polynomial-size restriction is not built into the minimization.

The circuits compared at different input lengths are completely nonuniform. They need not have computable descriptions or be produced by the machine deciding \(L\). The E condition applies to the single language whose membership functions are being computed. There is no extra algorithmic requirement to find a smallest circuit or compute its size.

The same language and the same positive exponent \(\delta\) must work for arbitrarily large lengths. A different hard function chosen independently at each length qualifies only if the resulting family has a single E decider. The displayed claim is equivalent to the existence of such an \(L\) with
\[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)}{n}>0.\]
Its negation says that every \(L\in\mathrm E\) has \(\log_2(S_3(f_{L,n})+2)/n\to0\). Thus a refutation permits the sublinear exponent and its rate to depend on \(L\), and does not require an effective procedure for constructing the circuits. The phrase exponential lower bound is interpreted at the class-noncontainment level; the source does not spell out an almost-every-length quantifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence statement. A proof must establish one E language, its uniform deterministic exponential-time bound and a positive constant exponent for a lower bound against every allowed circuit at infinitely many lengths. A refutation must prove sublinear logarithmic circuit size, as specified in the definitions, for every E language. Counting hard functions without an E evaluator, restricting bottom fan-in or monotonicity, allowing an oracle in the evaluator, or proving only a square-root-exponent lower bound is insufficient.

cards.title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
cards.why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.

The search is bounded and cited proofs were not independently verified.

importance.reason: A major longstanding structural conjecture in query complexity, asserting a universal quadratic barrier for randomized recognition across all nontrivial monotone graph properties.

sentences: A monotone graph property is invariant under vertex renaming and cannot be destroyed by adding edges.
The conjecture says every nonconstant such property needs a quadratic number of adjacency queries even with randomized error at most one third.
The query bound is worst-case over graphs and random choices, while the error guarantee holds separately for each graph.
Zero-error expected-cost lower bounds and the solved quantum analogue concern distinct computational models.
A resolution would establish or refute a universal information barrier for randomized exact graph recognition.

cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E_n\) be the set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \([n]\). An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) describes a finite simple undirected graph: \(x_e=1\) means e is an edge. Every one of the \(2^{\binom n2}\) assignments is a valid input. A graph property is a function \(P:\{0,1\}^{E_n}\to\{0,1\}\) invariant under every permutation of the vertices, with the permutation acting on each edge’s two endpoints. Monotone means \(x_e\le y_e\) for every e implies \(P(x)\le P(y)\). Nonconstant means some input has value 0 and another has value 1; for monotone P the empty graph has value 0 and the complete graph value 1. No monotonicity across different vertex counts is imposed. A deterministic query tree is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes name edges, whose outgoing branches carry the possible queried bits, and whose leaves carry output bits. On input x it follows the branch specified by each queried \(x_e\). Its cost on x is the number of queries along that path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution \(\mu\), independent of x, on such trees. It has cost at most q if every tree with positive probability has depth at most q. It computes P with error at most \(1/3\) when \(\Pr_{T\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\ge 2/3\) for every input x. Define \(R_{1/3}(P)\) as the smallest such integer q. The distribution and trees may depend on P and n. Sampling, storage and all computation on previously obtained answers are uncharged; only queries revealing one adjacency bit are counted. There is no uniformity or efficient-construction requirement on the trees, and no description of P is part of the queried graph. Queries may be adaptive. Input distributions, promises that a no-instance is far from P, quantum access, certificates and other graph oracles are absent. Cost is worst-case over both the graph and trees in the support, not expected over those choices. The only approximation allowed is the stated probability of an incorrect membership bit. In particular, a graph missing P by a single edge still requires the same success guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal lower-bound proposition. A positive answer requires one c and one \(n_0\) working for all the indicated graph properties and all \(n\ge n_0\). Its negation is: for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge 2\), there exist an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonconstant monotone graph property P on n vertices with \(R_{1/3}(P)<c n^2\). A refutation must establish this quantified failure, not just a constant-factor saving from querying every edge. A result only for zero-error randomized algorithms, deterministic algorithms, selected properties, or proximity testing does not by itself settle the bounded-error target.

context_blocks.text: Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.

cards.context:
Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.
