cards.definitions:
SAT is the language of satisfiable finite Boolean formulas built from variables, NOT, binary AND and binary OR. Fix the following binary prefix encoding: a variable with positive index i is 00 followed by 1^l 0 and the l-bit binary representation of i, where l is the bit length of i; NOT is 01 followed by one encoded formula; AND is 10 followed by two encoded formulas; OR is 11 followed by two encoded formulas. A valid string must encode exactly one complete formula. Invalid strings are outside SAT. Truth assignments map the finitely many variables occurring in a formula to Boolean values, with the usual truth tables for the three connectives.

The sentence \(\sigma\) is the usual finite-computation arithmetization of: there exist a deterministic Turing machine M and positive integers c,k such that, for every binary string x, M halts within \(c(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and outputs 1 exactly when x is in SAT, and 0 otherwise. Machines have a finite transition table, a two-way infinite tape, a finite tape alphabet containing the binary input symbols and blank, a start state, and accepting and rejecting halting states; each transition reads and writes one symbol, changes state, and moves the head by at most one cell. The input is written consecutively starting at the initial head position, with blank elsewhere. There is no oracle, advice or randomness. Finite strings, transition tables and computation histories are encoded by natural numbers. Standard effective encodings of these finite objects give ZFC-provably equivalent sentences, so the target is invariant under their choice. SAT is NP-complete, making this the conventional P = NP sentence.

ZFC means classical first-order set theory in the language of membership and equality, with extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set, infinity, foundation, choice, and the separation and replacement schemas for all first-order formulas with parameters. Arithmetic is interpreted on its natural numbers, with finite strings and machine computations encoded there. The notation \(\mathrm{ZFC}\vdash\tau\) means that there is a finite derivation of \(\tau\) using these axioms in a sound and complete classical first-order proof calculus with equality; equivalent standard calculi give the same derivable sentences. There is no proof-length bound, extra soundness axiom, oracle, or restriction to a weak fragment of arithmetic. Both unprovability assertions range over all finite derivations in the ordinary metatheory.

The question asks for actual syntactic independence, without building a consistency hypothesis into the proposition. A positive answer entails that ZFC is consistent; inconsistency would make both sentences derivable and hence make this independence claim false. If an argument assumes Con(ZFC) or stronger principles, those assumptions must remain explicit. Choosing ZFC makes the source's general independence discussion into one definite yes/no question; it does not claim that independence from every possible axiom system is equivalent.

context_blocks.text: Fortnow’s further-reading section directs readers to Aaronson’s survey on formal independence. The general source discussion does not select a single axiom system; the target here explicitly fixes full ZFC.

Aaronson distinguishes independence for weak logical theories from the unresolved question for strong theories encompassing ordinary mathematical reasoning. Conditional bounded-arithmetic results do not establish either unprovability assertion for full ZFC.

Oracle results change the computational model by allowing machines to query an additional language. Opposite relativizations or independence of an oracle formulation do not establish independence of the ordinary SAT sentence used here.

The target concerns finite formal derivations in a specified theory. It does not say that the arithmetic statement lacks a truth value, and it does not restrict the length or the mathematical methods of a permitted ZFC derivation.

Actual syntactic independence implies consistency of the named theory. An independence theorem stated only under an unproved consistency assumption has a different logical form, so such an assumption must remain explicit in any proposed answer.

A proof only about a weaker theory, bounded-length proofs, an oracle version, or an unrelated strengthened statement does not settle this target. An independence theorem conditional on consistency settles only that explicitly conditional version unless its assumption is also established.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.

cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.

cards.title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. At a randomized transition the machine may obtain one independent unbiased random bit, with this transition counted in its runtime. Success probability is over these internal bits for each fixed input, not over a distribution of graphs. BPP consists of binary languages for which such a machine has error at most \(1/3\) on every input and a polynomial worst-case clock over inputs and random outcomes. For \(\mathrm{GNI}\), acceptance is required with probability at least \(2/3\) when the encoding is valid and \(G\not\cong H\); it is at most \(1/3\) for isomorphic pairs and malformed strings. Distinct vertex counts form yes-instances for GNI. The output is only one membership bit, without a nonisomorphism certificate, quantum computation or interaction with another party. One machine and one polynomial must work at all graph sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\) or \(\mathrm{GNI}\notin\mathrm{BPP}\) in the model above. The positive case must supply one uniform polynomial-time bounded-error decider, or establish its existence, with the required probability bound on every input. The negative case must exclude every such randomized machine. Correctness only on typical graphs, an interactive verification protocol, a method with only expected polynomial time and no suitable clock conversion, or a restricted-model lower bound does not by itself settle this target.

context_blocks.text: Graph nonisomorphism asserts that no bijection of the vertex sets preserves adjacency. An isomorphism is an easily checked witness for the opposite answer; a failed attempt to find one does not certify nonisomorphism. The target requires a bounded probability of error on every graph pair, including highly symmetric instances.

Goldreich’s footnote uses graph nonisomorphism to contrast an interactive proof with a problem not known to have a BPP algorithm. The verifier in such a proof receives messages from a computationally unbounded party. The question here removes that assistance and asks about the verifier’s own randomized computation.

BPP is closed under complement: reversing the answer preserves its error bound and runtime. After checking that the encoding is valid, an algorithm for nonisomorphism can therefore be turned into one for isomorphism, and conversely. Validity checking is needed because both graph languages reject malformed strings. Thus this is exactly the randomized polynomial-time question for ordinary graph isomorphism, with its answer polarity reversed.

The deterministic and randomized targets are related but distinct. A deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider supplies a positive answer here. A negative answer here would exclude a deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider and, since isomorphism has efficiently checkable permutation witnesses, would imply P differs from NP. A positive answer here does not automatically derandomize the computation.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.

cards.title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
cards.formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
cards.why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

sentences: The problem asks for directed reachability to be decided simultaneously in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space.
One uniform deterministic machine must meet both bounds on every explicitly encoded graph and marked vertex pair.
No graph restrictions, randomness, advice or additional catalytic memory are allowed.
Separate efficient-time and small-space algorithms do not satisfy the joint requirement.
The target is equivalently inclusion of nondeterministic logspace in SC, and is weaker than L equaling NL.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Exercise 9 explicitly asks whether PATH is in SC and points out that Savitch’s theorem does not settle this. The small-space simulation uses superpolynomial time, while usual graph traversal uses much more than polylogarithmic space.

Barnes, Buss, Ruzzo and Schieber give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with space \(v/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log v})}\). This is sublinear but remains far larger than any fixed power of \(\log v\). Their introduction also separates lower bounds for restricted graph-exploration models from bounds for general Turing computation.

The 2025 paper studies quantum logspace on directed graphs with bounded path counts and reviews deterministic simultaneous bounds for such restricted instances. Its promises and computational model are different from an unrestricted deterministic reachability algorithm.

The February 2026 preprint trades ordinary workspace against an additional tape of catalytic memory. Catalytic storage is extra writable memory that must eventually be restored, and is absent from this card’s model; a small ordinary-workspace bound in that model is not the claimed SC containment.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.

sentences: A language in NP intersect coNP has short efficiently checkable certificates for both yes and no instances.
The question asks whether some such language still lies outside deterministic polynomial time.
Having two kinds of witnesses does not automatically tell an algorithm how to find either one.
The separation would identify difficulty independent of the asymmetric certification typical of NP-complete problems.
The project explores whether efficiently verifiable certainty on both sides can coexist with an intrinsically hard decision process.

cards.definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decided on every input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^k\) steps for fixed constants \(C,k\). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.

context_blocks.text: A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm P\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm P\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.

Specified uniform bit computation and an unconditional language lower bound; excluded confusion with promise and witness-search targets.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits

cards.why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a basic model of two layers of weighted Boolean decisions. An exponential lower bound with unrestricted real weights would establish a strong limit on this expressive shallow architecture for an explicitly verifiable computational task.

cards.definitions: A threshold gate on Boolean inputs \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) outputs one if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_i z_i\geq\theta\), where all weights \(w_i\) and the threshold \(\theta\) are arbitrary real numbers of either sign. An unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit on \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) consists of any finite number \(s\) of such gates applied to the original input bits, followed by one threshold output gate applied to their outputs. Arbitrary fan-in, fan-out and length-dependent weights are permitted; omitted inputs can have weight zero. Its size is \(s+1\), the number of threshold gates, not total weight magnitude or the number of bits encoding weights. Constants and direct input-to-output connections can be represented by additional threshold gates, changing size by at most \(n+1\), which does not alter exponential-size existence. Computation must agree with \(f_n\) on every input, with no approximation. The family is explicit in the definition of Section 1.5.1 of the source: there exist a polynomial \(q\) and a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \(f_n(x)=1\) precisely when some binary witness \(y\) with \(|y|\leq q(n)\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). Verifier cost is measured on a standard bit Turing machine. Neither circuit weights nor circuits are required to be uniform or polynomially bounded. The exponential target is interpreted as \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for all sufficiently large input lengths, with one fixed positive exponent coefficient.

context_blocks.text: Research Problem 11.40 asks for an exponential lower bound for unrestricted depth-two threshold circuits. The preceding discussion obtains strong bounds under restrictions on the weights; dropping such restrictions is the point of the question.

The source explicitly defines “explicit” in Section 1.5.1 through polynomial-time verification, corresponding to NP. Requiring the chosen function to lie in P would add a stronger condition that is not imposed here. Counting the existence of hard truth tables without this uniform verification condition would miss the intended explicit lower bound.

Chen’s 2018 paper describes even superpolynomial unrestricted depth-two threshold lower bounds for NEXP as a major frontier and develops conditional implications. Those implications do not supply the unconditional exponential lower bound for an NP family required by this card.

cards.title: Black-Box Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.

source_formulation.text: The main statement, which we will call here ‘the Black-Box Hypothesis’, remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 4

cards.why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.

Conditional consequences quoted from these sources were checked for scope, not independently reproved.

sentences: The Black-Box Hypothesis compares access to a Boolean circuit’s code with access to its input-output behavior.
It concerns total semantic properties that a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm decides correctly on every circuit representation.
The proposed black-box algorithm receives unary input length and circuit-size bounds and may make adaptive evaluations of the function.
Its total running time, including queries, must be polynomial in those bounds with error at most one third on each input.

cards.definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge0\), a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) has the length-\(2^n\) truth table \(\operatorname{tt}(f)\), ordered lexicographically by input. A property is an arbitrary family \(F=(F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of total Boolean predicates on these tables. It need not be invariant under permutations of the input variables or table positions. Its semantic character means that two circuits computing the same \(n\)-input function have the same required property value.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. Wires may share gate outputs; unrestricted depth is allowed. Unused designated input vertices are retained. Its size \(s(C)\) is the number of vertices plus wires, and its computed function is \(f_C\). Define \(s(f)=\min\{s(C):f_C=f\}\). Counting input vertices is a harmless explicit convention because the black-box resource bound includes \(n\).

Descriptions list all vertices in topological order, their types and earlier incoming indices, followed by the output index; integers use self-delimiting binary fields. This gives a polynomial-time parsable encoding of length polynomial in \(s(C)+1\), including all \(n\) input vertices. Any fixed encoding with these properties gives the same polynomial-time target. Malformed descriptions are rejected.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{wbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,k\) such that \(A\) halts on every input and every random-bit sequence within \(c(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is description length, and
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr[A(\operatorname{desc}(C))=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f_C))]\ge2/3.\]
The same machine must work across all sizes and arities and on every representation of a function, including padded or redundant circuits. The acceptance probabilities for different representations need not be equal; each must give the correct Boolean property value with the stated error bound.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{bbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(d,\ell\) such that \(B^f(1^n,1^m)\) halts within \(d(n+m+1)^\ell\) steps on every random-bit sequence, and
\[\forall n\ge0\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\ \forall m\ge1,\quad m\ge s(f)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[B^f(1^n,1^m)=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f))]\ge2/3.\]
Here \(m\) is an integer upper bound, not necessarily the minimum circuit size. Both parameters are in unary. A query consists of an explicitly written \(n\)-bit string \(x\); the oracle returns \(f(x)\) in one step. Writing and manipulating the query counts toward time. Invalid-length queries return a fixed zero bit. Queries may be adaptive, and all computation between queries also counts. Thus the bound is on running time, not merely the number of oracle calls. The same machine and polynomial work for all valid bounds \(m\). If \(m<s(f)\), no correctness is required, but the running-time bound remains.

Both machines use independent fair random bits, and all probabilities above are over those bits for each fixed input or oracle. They have no advice or other oracle. In the black-box case, \(f\) and the unary parameters are the only supplied information about the function; no circuit, truth table, distribution on circuits or special representation is given. The circuit-size promise in this definition does not turn \(F_n\) into a partial property: \(F_n\) is defined on every Boolean function.

The quantifiers allow \(A,B\) and their polynomial constants to depend on \(F\). The conclusion is existence of a suitable \(B\) for every white-box decidable property, not an additional requirement of an effective procedure that transforms arbitrary machine descriptions into black-box algorithms.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal implication. A proof must establish a uniform black-box algorithm with the stated total running-time and pointwise error guarantees for every total semantic property in white-box BPP. A refutation must specify one such property and a correct white-box BPP algorithm and prove that no black-box BPP algorithm decides it under the supplied-size-bound model. A property defined only on a promised family of circuits, a distinction between two encodings of the same function, or a lower bound only for nonadaptive queries does not alone meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2017 source identifies this as the total-property form of the scaled-down Rice’s theorem conjecture originating in work on program obfuscation. It distinguishes the still-open hypothesis from conditional counterexamples to a promise version; those counterexamples do not decide a property on every circuit.

The authors prove consequences of particular kinds of hypothetical counterexamples, including ones with highly sensitive low-complexity functions. These are conditional implications for circuit satisfiability, rather than a general proof or disproof of the hypothesis.

The 2021 paper retains the original hypothesis as open and studies other combinations of analysts and represented computations. Its positive results for restricted circuit analysts, and its equivalence involving nondeterministic circuits as boxes, change the computational models and do not settle ordinary circuits with uniform BPP analysts.

The cost of black-box computation includes the unary circuit-size bound. This avoids demanding a polynomial-in-arity algorithm for properties of functions whose smallest circuits are already exponentially large, and makes the two kinds of access comparable.

cards.definitions: An MCSP input is the complete truth table \(t\in \{0,1\}^{2^{n}}\) of a Boolean function on \(n\ge 1\) input bits, in lexicographic order, together with a nonnegative integer size threshold s in binary. It is accepted if some Boolean circuit of size at most s computes that function. Circuits are finite acyclic graphs over binary AND and OR, unary NOT, input variables and constants 0,1, with one designated output and unrestricted sharing. Size counts noninput gates, including constant gates. The total encoded input length counts the truth table, threshold and delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. NP-hardness means that for every language L in NP there is a deterministic polynomial-time map r such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(r(x)\in\)MCSP. NP consists of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup _{k\ge 1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{k}}); \mathrm{P}\)/poly consists of languages decided by families of Boolean circuits whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in input length, with no uniformity condition on their construction. \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly means that some language in EXP has no such polynomial-size circuit family.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the conditional implication or its logical negation in these exact reduction and circuit models. Deriving only \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\) or \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly is a weaker consequence. A theorem for a restricted reduction class or for partial, promise or approximate circuit minimization does not prove the stated implication.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?

cards.definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b- 1; a\) terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(\mathrm{P}(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.title: A steady stream of digits
context_blocks.text: For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

context_blocks.title: The finite description is not the resource bound
context_blocks.text: The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

context_blocks.title: Why sources also say linear time
context_blocks.text: Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

context_blocks.title: What the partial results establish
context_blocks.text: Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The input representation matters
context_blocks.text: The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

cards.title: UNSAT multi-prover proofs with efficient SAT-oracle provers
cards.formal:
Does UNSAT have a classical multi-prover interactive proof with a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and uniform probabilistic polynomial-time honest provers that may query SAT? The verifier has no oracle. For one fixed protocol, every unsatisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\) when all provers are honest, while every satisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\) for every collection of computationally unbounded, noncommunicating classical provers.

This restores the complement bar on SAT in the original Conjecture 6.2. The imported card lost that bar and incorrectly named SAT as the language to be proved; the oracle available to the honest provers is still SAT.
cards.why: This asks whether the output of a solver for an NP-complete problem can be checked using only the computational power of that solver. It connects the trustworthiness of hard computation to interactive proofs and to the limits of reductions between NP and total search.

importance.reason: A longstanding program-checking question for the canonical NP-complete problem, with links to interactive proofs, total search and worst-case hardness. The honest-prover resource restriction exposes a substantial structural gap beyond ordinary coNP interactive proofs.

sentences: The actual source asks for interactive proofs of unsatisfiability, with several noncommunicating classical provers.
Honest provers must run in randomized polynomial time with SAT-oracle access, while the verifier is polynomial-time and has no oracle.
Soundness must hold against all computationally unbounded classical cheating strategies.
The target is tied to checking a purported SAT solver and remains distinct from ordinary interactive proofs with unrestricted honest provers.
The imported SAT label lost a complement bar; the card restores UNSAT and records the correction explicitly.

cards.definitions:
Fix a binary encoding of finite Boolean formulas as explicitly written AND/OR/NOT expression trees with binary variable identifiers and delimiters. Its full bit length is \(n\). SAT consists of the well-formed formulas having a satisfying assignment. UNSAT consists of the well-formed formulas having none. The verifier rejects malformed encodings deterministically before any interaction. This convention differs from the literal language complement of SAT only on efficiently recognizable malformed strings and does not change the existence question. All participants receive the same input formula.

A protocol specifies one constant number \(k\ge2\) of provers, one uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing-machine verifier \(V\), and one honest probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(P_i^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). All are fixed finite programs, independent of input length. There is one polynomial bound \(p(n)\) on the verifier’s total computation and number of fair random bits, the number of message exchanges, and the total communication bits. Each honest prover has polynomial total running time in \(n\) throughout the protocol, on every random tape and within the communication bounds; its bound may depend on the fixed protocol. Writing SAT queries and processing their answers are charged, while the oracle returns one exact satisfiability bit per invocation. Malformed oracle queries return 0. Queries are allowed to depend on the prover’s local transcript and private randomness. There is no nonuniform advice or additional oracle.

The verifier uses private random bits and sends classical messages to individually addressed provers. Each prover’s response may depend only on the common input, its identity, its own received and sent messages, and its internal random bits and state. It cannot see messages exchanged with another prover except information that the verifier explicitly forwards. Provers cannot communicate with one another once interaction starts. Classical shared randomness independent of the verifier’s private randomness is allowed: for the honest protocol, a common uniform seed of polynomial length, together with independent private fair bits, suffices to specify it. There is no entanglement or quantum communication. No constant bound on the number of rounds is required.

The verifier must respect its polynomial clock even when provers cheat. Messages longer than its prescribed bounds, invalidly formatted messages or failure to answer a requested message cause rejection. Soundness quantifies over all classical prover strategies subject only to the communication and information restrictions. Cheating provers may have unlimited computation, arbitrary input-dependent prearranged strategies and shared classical randomness; they are not limited to SAT-oracle polynomial time. For fixed input and fixed private/shared prover randomness, a strategy gives each response as a function of that prover’s local transcript. Equivalently, randomized strategies are distributions over such deterministic strategy tuples. The provers have no access to the verifier’s private bits except through the messages they receive.

Let \(\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1,\ldots,P_k)(F)=1]\) mean the probability that the verifier accepts formula \(F\), over the verifier’s fair bits and the honest or cheating strategy’s randomness as applicable. The requirements are
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{UNSAT},\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^{\mathrm{SAT}},\ldots,P_k^{\mathrm{SAT}})(F)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \forall(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*),\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*)(F)=1]\le1/3.\]
One fixed tuple of honest algorithms must meet completeness for all yes-inputs. The soundness bound holds even for cheating strategies tailored separately to each no-input. Polynomial time is worst-case over randomness and allowed transcripts, not merely expected time. These constant error thresholds fix the ordinary bounded-error convention; no cryptographic hardness assumption or computational soundness restriction is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated protocol. A positive answer must specify its verifier, finite prover count, honest SAT-oracle algorithms and polynomial bounds, and prove completeness and soundness against every permitted cheating strategy. A negative answer must exclude every such fixed protocol, rather than one round bound or construction. A proof system with unbounded honest provers, a verifier that can itself query SAT, efficient-cheater-only soundness, or quantum/entangled provers does not answer this target. A relativized counterexample or a consequence conditional on an unproved class separation does not refute the unrelativized statement. Exact probability inequalities and asymptotic bounds apply; numerical approximation tolerance is irrelevant.

source_formulation.text: Conjecture 6.2 asks for a multi-prover interactive proof of the complement of SAT whose honest provers use probabilistic polynomial time with a SAT oracle.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Conjecture 6.2; visually verified complement bar restored after a text-extraction error

context_blocks.text: A satisfying assignment can be checked directly, and a SAT oracle can find such an assignment by deciding successive partial assignments. Consequently, the analogous efficient-prover statement for satisfiable formulas is straightforward. Certifying unsatisfiability is the substantive target; losing the complement bar changes the mathematical question.

Several provers can be cross-examined while being prevented from coordinating their answers during the interaction. The verifier remains computationally weak. The extra requirement here is that honest provers can prepare all their responses using only randomized polynomial time with SAT decisions, while dishonest provers receive no computational restriction.

The source relates this protocol to SAT program checking. In that setting a randomized polynomial-time checker can query a purported solver: it must flag an error with high probability if the answer on the designated input is wrong, and accept the answer with high probability if the solver is correct on all inputs. Correctness only on the designated input need not force acceptance.

Fortnow states the characterization connecting checkability to efficient-oracle-prover multi-prover proofs for a language and its complement. The SAT side is straightforward; the UNSAT side is the unresolved requirement. Ordinary interactive proofs for coNP with unrestricted honest prover computation do not establish this stronger efficiency statement.

Mahmoody and Xiao record the implication \(\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{TFNP}}\Rightarrow\mathrm{SAT}\text{ is checkable}\). Here TFNP consists of total search relations with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time-checkable solutions, and the antecedent means that a randomized polynomial-time SAT algorithm can use an oracle returning any valid solution of one such relation. The antecedent is not known, so this is a conditional connection rather than a protocol satisfying the card.

The 2025 range-avoidance paper explicitly retains SAT checkability as open in its §2.4 and recalls the same conditional implication. Its new protocols concern range avoidance and circuit image sizes; that discussion does not assert the requested UNSAT protocol.

cards.title: Excluding one-sided randomized quasilinear-time log-space SAT
cards.formal:
Is it true that no uniform randomized random-access algorithm decides Boolean satisfiability with one-sided error while using both quasilinear time and logarithmic workspace? More precisely, for every integer \(k\ge0\), is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{RTISP}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k,\ \log_2(N+2)\right]?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length. The two bounds hold simultaneously for one machine on every input and every sequence of coin flips. The error is allowed only on satisfiable inputs: each is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), whereas an unsatisfiable input is never accepted.
cards.why: This asks whether the known obstruction to extremely fast, very low-memory SAT algorithms survives useful one-sided randomness. An unconditional answer would advance lower bounds for a central NP-complete problem in a general computation model.
cards.status_note: Source-open for the one-sided-error direction in the original Problem 5. The full source column, Diehl–van Melkebeek’s 2006 main statements and §§2.1–2.2 model conventions, and the 2021 Main Theorem 3/Definition 1 were read. The checked randomized results concern the opposite error direction or larger quantified/verification classes. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of this exact randomized SAT target; this is not an exhaustive literature or independent proof certification.

importance.reason: A sharply stated frontier for unconditional SAT lower bounds: it asks to handle fresh random bits in a resource regime already excluded deterministically, while preserving the error direction used by incomplete randomized solvers.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary explicitly written satisfiability instance.
A candidate algorithm may use fresh random bits, logarithmic working memory and time n times a fixed polynomial in log n.
It must never accept an unsatisfiable formula and must accept each satisfiable formula with constant probability.
Both resource bounds hold for the same machine on every sequence of random choices.
The target is an unconditional lower bound against every such algorithm; known opposite-error and larger-class results do not settle it.

cards.definitions:
An input is an explicit Boolean 3-CNF formula: a conjunction of clauses, each containing at most three literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. The empty clause is false and the empty conjunction is true. An assignment gives a Boolean value to every variable occurring; the formula is satisfiable when some assignment makes it true. Variable identifiers, signs, all occurrences and clause delimiters are written in a fixed self-delimiting binary list encoding. Identifiers can be taken from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused identifiers permitted; \(N\) counts bits, not variables or clauses. Malformed encodings are no instances. There is no compressed formula or promise on the formula’s structure. The source explicitly permits 3-CNF satisfiability as its SAT target.

For definiteness, a random-access machine is a finite Turing-machine program with ordinary finite-alphabet work tapes and an address tape. When the address tape contains a binary index, one query step reads that indexed input bit; an out-of-range index returns a fixed endmarker. Writing, modifying and storing an address are charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only; all work tapes start blank. The total number of distinct work-tape cells visited, including the address tape and all temporary counters, is the workspace. This permits unrestricted repeated input access without charging the distance between input positions. Work-tape access uses ordinary moves. With only logarithmic work storage, the usual random-access work-memory or logarithmic-word variants can be simulated with polynomial-logarithmic time overhead and logarithmic space, so this quasilinear-time union is unchanged. There is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers, advice, oracle, external storage or extra catalytic tape.

At a random step the machine receives one fresh independent unbiased bit, at unit time cost. The random stream is available only in order and cannot be reread unless the machine stores the desired bits in its charged workspace. A random step is not a query to a random-access tape of reusable random bits. The machine eventually outputs accept or reject, without needing to output an assignment.

Write \(\ell_N=\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). Membership in the displayed RTISP class would mean that one fixed machine and positive integer constants \(C,D\) satisfy, on every input and every random stream,
\[\text{time}\le T_N=D(N+2)\ell_N^k,\qquad \text{visited work cells}\le C\ell_N.\]
The harmless \(N+2\) makes the bound total at small lengths. Constants and \(k\) may depend on the machine, but not on the formula. In particular, this is a worst-case bound, not an expected-time or high-probability resource guarantee. At most \(T_N\) random bits can be consumed. Acceptance probability can therefore be defined as the fraction of strings in \(\{0,1\}^{T_N}\) that make the machine accept, ignoring unused trailing bits. For every valid satisfiable formula this fraction is at least \(2/3\); for every unsatisfiable or malformed input it is zero. A fixed positive success constant in place of \(2/3\) is equivalent by a constant number of repetitions, preserving the resource form and error direction.

The conjecture quantifies over every fixed \(k,C,D\) and every finite program. It concerns the simultaneous time-and-space class: a fast algorithm with large memory and a separate slow logarithmic-space algorithm would not supply the forbidden machine. The randomness is internal to the algorithm; inputs are arbitrary, not drawn from a specified distribution.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonexistence claim. A positive answer must exclude every uniform randomized machine, every fixed logarithmic-space constant, and every fixed polynomial-logarithmic time factor, with the specified one-way coins and error direction. A negative answer must give one machine and fixed \(k,C,D\), prove its time and space bounds on every random branch, and prove zero acceptance on no instances and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes instance. Bounds for deterministic machines, the opposite one-sided error, quantified formulas with extra quantifier alternations, a selected family of SAT solvers or expected resource usage do not establish this assertion. Neither an unproved separation such as P ≠ NP nor a conditional lower bound settles the unconditional target. The conclusion and probabilities have their exact stated meanings; no numerical approximation tolerance applies.

source_formulation.text: Problem 5 asks to rule out a randomized SAT algorithm using n times a fixed polynomial in log n time and logarithmic space, with possible error on satisfiable inputs only.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Problem 5, retaining its explicit direction of one-sided error

context_blocks.text: Randomized search for a satisfying assignment may miss an assignment that exists, while an accepted assignment can be checked for correctness. This motivates the source’s error direction. The target nevertheless ranges over all decision algorithms with this error behavior, not just procedures that explicitly search for or output an assignment.

Logarithmic memory holds only a small number of indices and counters. The input can be read repeatedly, but the time bound permits only a polynomial-logarithmic amount of overhead beyond its length. Randomness supplies fresh choices without furnishing free reusable storage. All three features—input access, memory and access to coins—matter.

Diehl and van Melkebeek prove polynomial-strength randomized lower bounds for quantified Boolean formulas with at least two quantifier blocks. Their theorem’s restriction excludes plain existential satisfiability. Higher-level quantified formulas cannot simply be substituted for the SAT instances in this card.

Their one-sided lower bound for tautology yields a bound for SAT with the opposite permitted error: always accept a satisfiable formula, but possibly accept an unsatisfiable one. Complementing outputs switches both the language and the error side. It does not yield the requested lower bound for algorithms that never accept an unsatisfiable input.

The 2016 source explains why ordinary space-efficient derandomization does not already settle the question. Its polynomial running-time overhead is too large for the known deterministic time-space lower bounds to contradict the resulting SAT algorithm. A qualitative polynomial-time simulation does not preserve the near-linear time requirement.

The 2021 paper extends time-space lower bounds to problems with randomized or quantum verification. Its Main Theorem 3 concerns linear-time Merlin–Arthur and quantum Merlin–Arthur classes against randomized logarithmic-space machines. Such a verifier receives an additional proposed witness; lower bounds for those larger classes are not automatically lower bounds for SAT.

cards.title: Real quantifier alternation versus summation
cards.formal: For every fixed \(t\ge1\), does the truth problem for closed real-arithmetic sentences with at most \(t\) alternating quantifier blocks admit a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\), the existential theory of the reals with Boolean summation binders? Equivalently, is every fixed level of the real polynomial hierarchy contained in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) as defined below? The polynomial-time reduction and its degree may depend on \(t\); the number of real variables in each block is unrestricted. Either existential or universal first blocks are included.
cards.why: Alternating real quantifiers express geometric and optimization conditions beyond pure existence. Finite summation over Boolean choices adds a form of counting without introducing new real quantifier blocks. Comparing these resources would clarify whether a single strengthened existential theory captures all fixed levels of the real hierarchy.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked ISAAC 2024 Section 9 and its full preprint. The earlier Basu–Zell topological theorem has a different target, while later corrections to bounded-domain real hierarchies do not prove this unrestricted summation containment. Bounded subsequent-result checks through 2026-09-16 verified no resolution.

progress.text: Basu and Zell publish a real Toda analogue based on topological counting. Its oracle is not the summation-only existential theory in this card.
The ISAAC paper defines the summation-only class, proves its PSPACE upper bound, and asks in Section 9 whether it contains the fixed real-alternation levels.

category_assignment.reason: The question compares real-algebraic complexity classes and counting power.

importance.reason: The question asks whether a counting-like arithmetic extension can absorb all fixed levels of real quantifier alternation. It would organize a broad hierarchy of real-feasibility and geometric decision problems and distinguish the power of Boolean summation from the stronger succinct and product extensions.

sentences: The question asks whether all fixed levels of alternating real quantification reduce to one strengthened existential theory.
That target theory permits nested sums over Boolean dummy variables inside arithmetic terms.
Its real variables must remain explicitly listed, and it has no compact product binder.
The reductions operate on finite binary descriptions and may have a different polynomial bound for each fixed alternation level.
A positive answer would supply the specific counting-versus-alternation principle proposed in the 2024 source, distinct from earlier topological Toda analogues.

cards.definitions:
The source input is a closed prenex sentence \(Q_1X_1\cdots Q_sX_s\,\phi\), where \(0\le s\le t\), each \(X_j\) is a finite tuple of distinct real variables, consecutive \(Q_j\in\{\exists,\forall\}\) differ, and every quantified variable ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\). There are no free variables. The matrix \(\phi\) is a finite Boolean formula using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and comparisons \(u=v\), \(u<v\), or \(u\le v\). Its arithmetic terms are finite expression trees built from integer constants, variables, binary addition, subtraction and multiplication. Integers are encoded by a sign and ordinary binary magnitude; variable indices are binary integers. Fix a parenthesized prefix encoding over a finite alphabet for all tree nodes, operators, variable indices and tuple lists. Input size is the full bit length of this encoding. There is no shared-subexpression circuit, implicit large power, summation binder or succinct indexing in these source terms. Binary integer constants and subtraction can equivalently be expressed using the source papers’ constants \(0,1\) and ring operations with polynomial overhead.

A target \(\Sigma\text{-}\mathrm{ETR}\) instance is a closed sentence \(\exists y_1\cdots\exists y_m\,\psi\), where \(m\ge0\), \(\psi\) is a Boolean formula of the same comparisons, and its arithmetic expression trees additionally allow the binder \(\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}}u\). This denotes \(u[b:=0]+u[b:=1]\). The bound symbol \(b\) is a local dummy scalar variable, distinct from the existentially quantified real variables and from other active dummy variables; usual capture-free substitution fixes its semantics. Binders may be nested, and their body is stored once, so nesting can describe exponentially many summands. All free variables in terms must be among the explicitly listed \(y_j\) or in scope of a summation binder. A dummy value may occur as a number in a term but cannot select a variable name: an expression such as \(y_b\), with a value-dependent index, is forbidden. No product binder, Boolean-formula binder, arbitrary real constant, real exponentiation, extra real quantifier alternation or succinct circuit representation is allowed. The size counts the finite syntax including each binder and its body, rather than the fully expanded sum. Thus the number of distinct existential real variables is at most the target length.

A deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction is a single finite-program multitape Turing machine that, on each valid input string of length \(L\), outputs one valid target sentence within \(C_t(L+1)^{c_t}\) bit transitions and preserves truth in both directions. It uses no random bits, advice, real-arithmetic oracle or decision oracle. Output length and all construction work count. Constants \(C_t,c_t\) and the machine may depend on the fixed block bound \(t\), but not on a particular input. The target class \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\) consists of binary-string languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to truth of these target sentences. The real polynomial hierarchy here is the union of the analogous closures of the source truth problems over all fixed \(t\). Its definition does not allow the block bound to grow with the input length.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof providing a truth-preserving polynomial-time reduction for every fixed block bound \(t\), or a complete Lean proof that such a reduction fails for at least one fixed \(t\). The affirmative proof must respect the target’s explicit variable list and summation-only syntax. A PSPACE upper bound, a reduction to a language with product binders or exponentially indexed real variables, or a reduction to a topological counting oracle is insufficient by itself.

context_blocks.text: The source’s phrase “real version of Toda’s theorem” is followed by the precise question of containment in \(\exists\mathbb R^\Sigma\). This card uses that containment as its sole target. It does not ask for an unspecified analogue among other real-computation models.

The crucial target restriction is the absence of value-dependent variable indexing. The source distinguishes ordinary \(\Sigma\)-ETR from a stronger summation language capable of addressing exponentially many real variables.

The source proves that the summation class lies in PSPACE and contains ordinary existential real feasibility. By contrast, adding the corresponding compact product binder yields PSPACE-completeness. These bounds do not settle whether summation alone contains all fixed alternation levels.

Schaefer and Štefankovič define the discrete real hierarchy through truth of finitely encoded sentences and polynomial-time reductions. Their March 2025 revision corrects certain bounded-closed-domain claims. The present target uses unrestricted real domains and the full comparison signature, so it does not rely on the withdrawn bounded-domain equivalences.

Basu and Zell already proved a real analogue of Toda’s theorem using topological counting, namely Betti-number information, in a compact real-machine setting. That established theorem has a different oracle and model from the summation-only containment posed in 2024.

cards.title: Downward self-reducibility of PLS-complete problems
cards.formal:
Is every PLS-complete total search problem downward self-reducible with respect to the bit length of its input? Precisely, for every binary relation \(R\) that is PLS-complete under polynomial-time search many-one reductions, must there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time oracle algorithm that finds an \(R\)-solution on every input \(x\), using an oracle for the same relation \(R\) only on strings \(z\) with \(|z|<|x|\)? It must work for every valid choice of solutions returned by that oracle.

The SODA 2026 result identifies this universal statement with \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). This is an equivalence with an unresolved complexity-class equality, rather than an unconditional affirmative or negative resolution of the card.
cards.why: The question tests whether a recursive structure characterizes every representation of hard local search. The newer equivalence shows that its unconditional resolution would also resolve whether all PLS problems can be solved in polynomial time.
cards.status_note: Source-open as an unconditional yes/no target, with major subsequent classification: the SODA 2026 paper (published 7 January; open 2025 full manuscript Theorem 6 and §7.1) proves that every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if PLS=FP. Definitions 2.1–2.8 and the entire §7.1 conditional counterexample proof were read, along with the original ITCS definitions and Open Problem 3.4. This does not prove PLS≠FP, so no unconditional negative answer or archival resolution is claimed. Bounded later-work checks through 16 September 2026 found no matching unconditional resolution. No independent Lean formalization of the cited proof was performed.

progress.text: The source proves a canonical complete example is downward self-reducible, establishes that downward self-reducible TFNP lies in PLS, and poses the universal complete-problem question.

The full manuscript’s Theorem 6 and §7.1, published at SODA 2026, characterize the universal traditional self-reducibility statement exactly by \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\); the counterexample is conditional on inequality.

sentences: The target asks whether every PLS-complete total search relation can be solved using only shorter instances of itself.
Shorter means fewer bits in the full input encoding, and the reduction must work for every valid solution oracle.
The original paper proves the property for a canonical complete problem and places downward self-reducible total NP search in PLS.

Its conditional negative result is recorded as progress; the card retains the unconditional yes/no question.

cards.definitions:
A total NP search problem is a relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\{0,1\}^{*}\) with three properties. Every input \(x\) has at least one valid output \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); all such outputs have length at most one fixed polynomial \(p(|x|)\); and membership \(R(x,y)\) is decidable by a uniform deterministic algorithm in polynomial time in \(|x|+|y|\). The class of these relations is TFNP. Solving \(R\) means producing any one valid output on every input, not enumerating all outputs or selecting a preferred one. Inputs include every binary string; any malformed-instance convention must be specified as part of the relation and preserve totality.

A polynomial-time search many-one reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of uniform polynomial-time functions \(a(x)\) and \(b(x,y)\) such that
\[\forall x,y,\qquad Q(a(x),y)\Longrightarrow R(x,b(x,y)).\]
Thus every solution of the transformed instance must decode to a valid original solution. There is one oracle instance per reduction, with no promise about which solution will be returned.

PLS, polynomial local search, can be defined using the following standard circuit local-optimum problem. An instance explicitly describes positive integers \(m,r\) and Boolean circuits \(S:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(v:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{r}\). Circuit outputs of \(v\) are read as unsigned binary integers. Find a string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{m}\) such that
\[v(S(u))\le v(u).\]
Circuits are finite acyclic lists of AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with input and output wires explicitly listed; full descriptions, indices and dimensions count toward instance bit length. There is always a valid \(u\), for example any point maximizing \(v\) over the finite domain. On malformed circuit descriptions the only valid output is the empty string. This gives a total, polynomially balanced, efficiently verifiable relation. PLS consists of the TFNP relations reducible to this circuit problem by the reductions above; this is the usual polynomial-local-search class, equivalently presented by the source’s Sink-of-DAG complete problem. A relation \(R\) is PLS-complete if it is in PLS and every relation in PLS reduces to it. Completeness is not restricted to familiar combinatorial problems or any preferred encoding.

A solution oracle for \(R\) is any total selector \(O:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) satisfying \(R(z,O(z))\) for every \(z\). The selector need not be computable. Downward self-reducibility requires one deterministic oracle Turing machine \(A\) and constants \(C,d\ge1\) such that, for every valid selector \(O\) and every input \(x\), the computation \(A^O(x)\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) steps, outputs a valid \(R\)-solution for \(x\), and queries only strings shorter than \(x\). Query writing, answer reading and ordinary computation are charged; the oracle’s computation of an answer is not. Later queries may depend on earlier answers. Repeated queries receive the selector’s same answer. The machine must handle every selector, rather than assume a canonical or favorable solution. In particular, on the empty input it can make no query. All programs and polynomial bounds may depend on the fixed relation \(R\), but not on its individual input or the chosen selector.

“Smaller” means strictly fewer input bits, \(|z|<|x|\). It does not mean a smaller potential value, fewer circuit variables with a longer description, or a separately chosen well-founded measure. Queries must be to the identical encoded relation \(R\), not to an interchangeable PLS-complete problem. The total polynomial bound covers the one oracle computation; it does not presume that expanding all recursive oracle calls takes polynomial time.

In the known equivalence, \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\) is shorthand for: every relation in PLS has a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm producing a valid solution on every input. This does not identify a relation with a single-valued function. The question’s quantifier order is: for every PLS-complete relation, there exist a machine and polynomial bound that work for every input and every valid solution selector.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal statement for the stated many-one reductions and strict bit-length notion. A positive answer must establish downward self-reducibility for every PLS-complete relation. A negative answer must establish a PLS-complete relation for which no such oracle algorithm exists, with the completeness and nonexistence proofs both checked. It is equivalent to settle whether all PLS problems have polynomial-time solution algorithms, provided the equivalence is also supplied or imported as a proved Lean theorem. Merely proving the existing equivalence, assuming \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), or giving a counterexample conditional on that assumption does not answer the exact yes/no target. Nor does a result only about a broader size measure, a restricted family of encodings or one chosen complete problem. Asymptotic class and quantifier statements are exact; no numerical tolerance applies.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 3.4 asks whether every PLS-complete problem is downward self-reducible.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Problem 3.4, interpreted using the source’s traditional input-bit-length Definition 2.17; later equivalence recorded separately

context_blocks.text: A downward self-reduction turns a problem into calls to smaller instances of itself. For a total search problem, each call always has some valid answer, but a reduction cannot choose which answer it receives. This combines a recursive structure with a requirement of robustness to all solutions.

The original paper proves downward self-reducibility for a canonical PLS-complete problem and proves that every downward self-reducible TFNP problem belongs to PLS. These statements establish an important connection, but neither says that downward self-reducibility transfers through every completeness reduction.

Input representation matters because a polynomial-time reduction may increase bit length. A query that is smaller in one presentation need not remain smaller after translating back to another complete problem. The universal target includes all binary encodings satisfying the definitions, rather than only natural examples.

The later paper proves the exact equivalence: every PLS-complete problem is traditionally downward self-reducible if and only if \(\mathrm{PLS}=\mathrm{FP}\). Its §7.1 gives a PLS-complete relation whose downward self-reducibility would force a polynomial-time solver. Therefore, under \(\mathrm{PLS}\ne\mathrm{FP}\), the answer is no. The theorem does not prove that assumption.

The equivalence changes how the original question should be understood: a universal affirmative answer would settle the algorithmic complexity of all polynomial local search, while an unconditional negative answer would prove that some such total search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. The card keeps that unconditional target.

The 2026 paper also studies self-reductions that decrease a more general size measure. Its final discussion leaves a separate universal question for that broader notion. That question is not substituted for the original strict input-length formulation.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) perfect matching
cards.formal:
Does perfect-matching decision for general undirected graphs have nonuniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and logarithmic depth?

For each integer \(v\ge2\), let \(\mathrm{PM}_v:\{0,1\}^{\binom v2}\to\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the encoded graph has a perfect matching. The target is the existence of fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\) and circuits \((C_v)_{v\ge2}\) such that
\[\forall v\ge2,\quad |C_v|\le a(v+1)^b,\qquad\operatorname{depth}(C_v)\le d\lceil\log_2(v+2)\rceil,\]
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\binom v2},\qquad C_v(x)=\mathrm{PM}_v(x).\]
The gates have fan-in at most two, and negation is allowed. The circuits need not be generated uniformly, and the output is only the decision bit.
cards.why: Perfect matching is a central polynomial-time graph problem whose exact bounded-fan-in depth remains poorly understood. A negative answer would separate nonuniform NC-one from P/poly using a concrete polynomial-time task. A positive answer would put the decision problem at a much shallower level than the broad polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithms studied in most matching work.

The current bipartite NC claim is outside this card’s graph and depth target; its full proof was not independently verified. Bounded later-work searches found no matching general-graph nonuniform NC-one resolution. The status is source-open with these limits.
