cards.definitions:
A graph has vertex set \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and an arbitrary set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices as edges. It is simple, undirected and unweighted, with no promise of bipartiteness, planarity, bounded degree or a matching already known to exist. Its input bits are \(x_{ij}\) for \(1\le i<j\le v\), in lexicographic order; \(x_{ij}=1\) precisely when the edge is present. Every bit string of this length is a valid graph. The input length \(m=\binom v2\) is polynomially related to \(v\), so the polynomial-size and logarithmic-depth requirements have the same meaning with either parameter. The statement starts at \(v=2\); the fixed zero- and one-vertex cases do not affect the asymptotic question.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to exactly one selected edge. Consequently \(\mathrm{PM}_v=0\) for odd \(v\). The algorithmic target is to output one bit indicating existence, not to construct a matching, count matchings or decide a weighted exact-value variant.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with variable inputs, constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. A gate output can feed arbitrarily many later gates. The size \(|C|\) is the number of computational gates, and depth is the maximum number of such gates on a path to the output. Variable and constant inputs have depth zero and do not count toward size. Input handling here is entirely through the indicated input wires; no oracle, random bits, threshold gates or unbounded-fan-in AND/OR primitives are present. Correctness is exact on every assignment.

Nonuniform means that each \(C_v\) may be chosen independently; there is no computability, logspace generation or polynomial-time construction requirement on the sequence. The integers \(a,b,d\) must nevertheless be fixed across all graph orders. This is the usual nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) target. A circuit satisfying the logarithmic depth bound can be expanded into a tree of polynomial size, so the simultaneous size requirement causes no additional asymptotic restriction in this single-output bounded-fan-in setting.

Equivalently, \(\mathrm{PM}_v\) must have polynomial-size De Morgan formulas. Such a formula is a rooted tree of binary AND/OR gates with possibly negated variable leaves; each repeated occurrence of a variable is counted separately, and internal values cannot be shared. Formula balancing yields logarithmic depth from polynomial leaf size. A negative answer is failure of every polynomial formula bound for this fixed family, or equivalently that its minimum circuit depth is not \(O(\log v)\); a lower bound may be witnessed at arbitrarily large graph orders rather than at every order.

For source fidelity, the draft’s function \(\mathrm{Match}_v\) asks whether the maximum matching size is at least \(v/3+1\), interpreted as the integer threshold \(k_v=\lceil v/3+1\rceil\). The two decision families are equivalent for the present circuit class. To express a size-at-least-\(k\) question as perfect matching, when \(0\le k\le v/2\), add \(v-2k\) new vertices adjacent to every original vertex and to no new vertex. The enlarged graph has a perfect matching exactly when the original graph has a matching of size at least \(k\). Thresholds above \(\lfloor v/2\rfloor\) are constantly false. Conversely, for a graph on \(2q\) vertices with \(q\ge3\), adding \(q-3\) isolated vertices makes the source threshold \((3q-3)/3+1=q\), so its Match answer is exactly the original perfect-matching answer. Smaller graph orders and odd perfect-matching orders have fixed finite answers. These transformations copy input bits and add fixed adjacency bits with only linear growth in vertex count, and hence preserve the nonuniform logarithmic-depth question in both directions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated nonuniform circuit-family existence claim. A positive answer must establish polynomial size, logarithmic depth and exact correctness on every general graph with constants fixed across graph orders; a uniform construction is welcome but not required. A negative answer must prove that no such family exists, equivalently that perfect matching has no polynomial-size De Morgan formula family. A lower bound only for monotone circuits, a polylogarithmic-depth upper bound, a bipartite-only result or a quasipolynomial size bound is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source places the matching question immediately after its general polynomial-size versus logarithmic-depth question. It proves a linear depth lower bound for monotone matching circuits, where negative occurrences are forbidden. That restriction is absent from the present target, so the monotone theorem does not answer it.

The source names a matching-size threshold rather than perfect matching. The explicit transformations in the definitions justify retaining the inherited perfect-matching title without silently attributing that exact wording to the draft.

The 2017 general-graph algorithm achieves polylogarithmic parallel time using quasipolynomially many processors. This is an important deterministic upper bound, but neither its depth nor its processor count meets the NC-one target.

The July 2026 revision claims deterministic NC algorithms for bipartite matching, including weighted and search variants. Even accepting the stated theorem, bipartite graphs and polylogarithmic depth do not give the general-graph logarithmic-depth decision family requested here.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
cards.definitions: Encode symbols \(0,1,2\) by \(00,01,10\), respectively, using a fixed ordered pair of bits for each input position. A circuit for length \(n\) is a finite acyclic directed Boolean circuit with \(2n\) ordered input bits and \(2n\) ordered output bits. Its non-input gates are binary AND, binary OR, unary NOT and optional constant-0 or constant-1 gates. Each such gate, including a constant gate, contributes one to size. Fan-out is unrestricted. Wires and output designations have no separate cost, and the same gate or input can feed multiple gates and outputs. The circuit is deterministic. It must be correct on every concatenation of valid input encodings; behavior on any input containing a pair \(11\) is unrestricted. For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1,2\}^n\), let \(i_1<\cdots<i_m\) be exactly the indices where \(a_i\ne2\). The required output encodes \(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}\) followed by \(n-m\) copies of \(2\). This definition includes \(m=0\) and \(m=n\). In particular, it preserves the relative order of a \(0\) and a \(1\); it does not sort them against each other. All output positions must be produced by one circuit and their gates are counted jointly. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum permitted circuit size for this promise function. The quantifiers are \(\exists C\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\exists\mathcal C_n\), with \(|\mathcal C_n|\le Cn\) and exact correctness on all valid inputs. The circuit may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and no algorithm constructing \(\mathcal C_n\) is required. The circuit may compute on the individual encoding bits; it is not restricted to comparing or routing indivisible records.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(s(n)\le Cn\) for some universal \(C\) and all \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation \(\forall C\ge1\;\exists n\ge1,\ s(n)>Cn\). The negative statement rules out every nonuniform family in the defined unrestricted Boolean model; a lower bound for comparators or indivisible-record routing does not suffice. A conditional result under an additional conjecture settles only that conditional version. A positive answer must retain the original order of the \(0\)s and \(1\)s, with an exact linear size bound rather than a bound multiplied by an unbounded iterated-logarithm factor.
cards.why: This is an elementary deterministic rearrangement whose output preserves an arbitrary binary subsequence. Its sequential simplicity contrasts with the difficulty of arranging all output bits in a fixed circuit. Resolving linear circuit size would sharpen the boundary between data movement with input-dependent access and unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean computation.

importance.reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.

references.title: Optimal Sorting Circuits for Short Keys
references.locator: SODA 2022, pages 3583–3629, online 5 January 2022; checked arXiv:2102.11489v2, 7 November 2021, Introduction, Theorem 1.1 and following explicit non-stability discussion

progress.text: Regan poses the linear-size circuit question for the exact stable ternary function.

The checked v2 of Asharov–Lin–Shi distinguishes its non-stable compaction construction from stable compaction and separates unrestricted Boolean gates from the indivisibility restriction. The work appeared at SODA 2021 and subsequently in SIAM Journal on Computing in 2022.
Lin and Shi’s SODA 2022 paper improves short-key sorting depth; the checked November 2021 manuscript’s Theorem 1.1 and accompanying discussion do not promise stability.

context_blocks.text: Regan’s July 2007 problem defines precisely the order-preserving movement of all dummy symbols to the right. The present two-bit encoding and complete Boolean basis make its nonuniform linear-size target explicit.

Ordinary ternary sorting discards the order between retained zeros and ones. Stable compaction must preserve that binary sequence, so a circuit that only counts occurrences of the three symbols computes a different function.

Asharov, Lin and Shi obtain improved Boolean circuits for compaction and sorting short keys, but their construction deliberately does not preserve stability. Their discussion distinguishes unrestricted Boolean computation from the indivisible-payload model used in some stable-compaction lower bounds.

Lin and Shi’s SODA 2022 work improves the depth of short-key sorting circuits while retaining near-linear size bounds with iterated-logarithm factors in the relevant short-key regime. Its Introduction explicitly states that the sorting is not stable. This result therefore does not provide a linear-size circuit for the stable ternary function.

The checked literature also discusses conditional lower bounds based on the Li–Li network-coding conjecture. Such conditional bounds and lower bounds for restricted data-movement models are not unconditional impossibility results for this card.

sentences: Stable ternary compaction moves every 2 to the end while preserving the order of all zeros and ones.
The question asks whether each input length admits an exact Boolean circuit of size proportional to that length.
Circuits may have arbitrary depth and fan-out and may compute freely on the fixed two-bit alphabet encoding.
Non-stable compaction and ordinary ternary sorting do not retain the binary sequence required in the answer.
The checked short-key sorting advances and conditional or restricted lower bounds do not resolve this nonuniform linear-size question.

cards.title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[L(g\circ f)\ge\alpha L(g)L(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
cards.why: A formula for a composition can substitute an inner computation wherever an outer input is used, multiplying the leaf counts. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.

A bounded later-work search did not identify a proof or refutation of this exact all-function constant-loss formula-size version. Its strong quantitative choice follows the book’s display and is distinguished from the original depth question and relaxed KRW variants. The source-open label is limited by this formulation-specific literature review.

importance.reason: A structural conjecture about formula composition that could turn local lower bounds into stronger general formula lower bounds.

sentences: The selected KRW variant asks whether minimum formula size under block composition is always within a constant factor of the product of the two minimum sizes.
Both functions can be arbitrary nonconstant Boolean functions, and the inner one is applied to disjoint input blocks.
Formulas use binary AND and OR with negation, count variable occurrences, and cannot share intermediate computations.
The constant must work for every function and dimension, so dimension-dependent losses do not suffice.
The original depth conjecture and recent results for strengthened communication tasks are related but distinct statements.

cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(r\), a total Boolean function is a map \(h:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\). Nonconstant means that it takes both values on its domain; it need not depend on every designated input coordinate. A De Morgan formula for \(h\) is a finite rooted tree whose internal operations are binary AND, binary OR, and unary NOT, and whose leaves are input variables or the constant bits zero and one. Its value is obtained by the usual Boolean operations from leaves to the root. It must compute \(h\) exactly on every input, with no randomness or promise on input values. There are no parity, threshold, arbitrary truth-table or unbounded-fan-in gates.

Formula size is the number of occurrences of input variables among its leaves. Positive and negated occurrences both count, and different occurrences of the same variable count separately. Constant leaves are free and can be eliminated from an optimum for a nonconstant function. NOT operations can be pushed onto variables without changing this measure. The minimum over all such formulas is \(L(h)\); it is a finite positive integer for nonconstant \(h\). No internal value can be shared between two parent operations: such reuse would produce a circuit rather than a formula.

The composed function has exactly \(mn\) designated coordinates \(x^{(j)}_i\), with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Block coordinates are distinct and unconstrained. The same inner function \(f\) is applied to every block, and its outputs, in block order, become the inputs of \(g\). The composition symbol here means this block operation, not ordinary composition of two maps with the same domain. Both functions and their composition may be specified by arbitrary finite truth tables, and no uniformity, polynomial-time evaluability, or monotonicity is assumed.

Since both functions are nonconstant, every Boolean vector supplied to \(g\) can be realized by some collection of blocks, and the composition is nonconstant. The usual substitution bound gives \(L(g\circ f)\le L(g)L(f)\). The question is whether the ratio to that upper bound is bounded away from zero uniformly over all functions and dimensions. Equivalently, is the infimum of these positive ratios strictly positive? This infimum need not be attained. Restricting \(0<\alpha\le1\) is equivalent.

The negation says that for every positive \(\alpha\), some pair and dimensions have ratio smaller than \(\alpha\). Thus a single saving relative to exact multiplication, or even failure of one proposed constant, is insufficient to refute the claim. Allowing constant functions with the convention \(L(h)=0\) would add only trivial inequalities; their exclusion makes the ratio formulation well-defined. Minimum depth, which counts gates along a longest path, is a different measure from the number of leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the constant-loss formula-size statement. A positive answer must establish one strictly positive factor for every permitted pair and dimensions. A negative answer must establish ratios arbitrarily close to zero, not merely a finite violation of equality or an unbounded additive saving in formula depth. Bounds for almost all functions, for special inner functions, for monotone formulas, or for a stronger communication search task do not alone prove the all-function claim. A composition inequality with a loss depending on either dimension, even polylogarithmically, is a weaker result unless upgraded to the fixed constant required here.

context_blocks.text: The book displays an absolute multiplicative constant in Conjecture 5.13. Its accompanying footnote also permits investigation of weaker losses and typical-function variants. The title and acceptance criterion identify which of those possibilities this record actually asks for.

The 1995 paper’s Open Question 4.1 asks about depth under composition and records examples with a growing additive loss in that measure. Those depth examples are not, by themselves, counterexamples to a constant-factor statement about minimum formula leaf count. The original paper and the later size formulation must be distinguished.

The 2023 paper explicitly distinguishes the original depth conjecture from the formula-size variant. Its Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2 prove composition bounds involving a separate inner-function complexity measure and dimension-dependent losses. Those theorems give important restricted comparisons without supplying the universal constant asserted in this card.

The 2025 STACS result concerns strong composition of communication relations: in addition to finding a differing input bit, the answer must lie in a block where the two inner-function outputs differ. That added requirement makes a different search task. The paper explicitly says its lower bounds do not directly translate into ordinary formula-depth lower bounds, and they also do not establish the present size inequality.

cards.title: A counting characterization of P with NP access
cards.formal:
Does there exist one total counting function \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) such that
\[\mathrm P^f=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}?\]
The oracle for \(f\) returns its exact nonnegative integer value in binary. Both sides are classes of decision problems with deterministic, adaptive polynomial-time oracle access. This asks about the ordinary, unrelativized classes; no auxiliary oracle or complexity separation is assumed.
cards.why: The question asks whether existential search has a precise counting counterpart at the level of computational power. Resolving it would clarify the boundary between deciding existence, counting witnesses and the polynomial hierarchy, while a negative answer would also separate P from NP.
cards.status_note: Source-open: Fortnow’s 18 August 2021 manuscript, §6.5/Conjecture 6.3, explicitly poses the unrelativized equality and the weaker containment question. Theorem 1.1 and §§2–4 of the 2009 Theory of Computing paper were read for the hierarchy comparison. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification. The equivalence of the two simulation requirements and the P=NP observation are elementary editorial consequences of the stated definitions, not new attributed theorems.

progress.text: Toda’s containment \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\mathrm P^{\#\mathrm P}\), with a short complete proof published by Fortnow in 2009, explains the strength available from unrestricted complete counting.
Conjecture 6.3 isolates the existence of a potentially weaker counting function with exactly NP-oracle polynomial-time power; the source also records the weaker hierarchy-bounded containment as open.

importance.reason: A structural comparison of two central forms of computation: NP-oracle decision and exact witness counting. Its connection to the polynomial hierarchy and the consequence of a negative answer make it substantial beyond one representation or reduction.

sentences: The target asks for one #P counting function whose polynomial-time oracle power is exactly P with an NP oracle.
The count is an exact nonnegative integer returned in binary, and oracle queries may be adaptive.
The same function must allow SAT decisions while itself being computable using SAT queries.
Complete counting can already capture the whole polynomial hierarchy, so choosing a weaker count is a substantive requirement.
The question concerns ordinary complexity classes, separately from the source’s request for a relativized counterexample.

cards.definitions:
All inputs and oracle queries are finite binary strings. Write \(|x|\) for the full bit length, and let \(\mathbb N\) include zero. A function \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathbb N\) belongs to \(\#\mathrm P\) if there are one deterministic polynomial-time predicate \(V(x,y)\) and one polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable length function \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that
\[f(x)=\bigl|\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\}\bigr|\]
for every string \(x\). Each witness string is counted once. This is an exact count, not a signed difference of counts, an approximation, a parity bit or a mere indication of nonemptiness. In particular, \(f(x)\le2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has polynomial length; zero is encoded as the one-bit string 0.

Use uniform deterministic multitape oracle Turing machines. A machine has one finite program independent of input length, a read-only input tape and ordinary work, query and answer tapes. It writes a query string \(z\), invokes the fixed oracle and receives the canonical binary expansion of \(f(z)\). The oracle's internal computation is not charged; writing queries, reading answer bits and all subsequent computation are charged. The oracle response is exact. The machine must halt on every input of length \(n\) in at most \(C(n+1)^d\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,d\). It may make polynomially many queries, and later queries may depend on earlier answers. There is no advice, randomness, nondeterminism or second oracle. The union over such machines defines the language class \(\mathrm P^f\); different languages may use different programs and polynomial bounds, but all use the same \(f\).

For the decision oracle, fix an explicit binary encoding of Boolean formulas as finite AND/OR/NOT expression trees with variable identifiers. SAT returns 1 exactly for a well-formed satisfiable formula, and returns 0 on an unsatisfiable formula or malformed string. The whole formula is written explicitly, including identifiers and delimiters. Since SAT is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) here means \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{SAT}}\). An SAT-oracle machine receives one exact decision bit per query; it has the same uniformity, adaptive access and polynomial running-time convention. \(\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) denotes the analogous functions computed by machines that output a finite binary string instead of a decision bit.

The displayed equality has the equivalent concrete requirements
\[\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm P^f\qquad\text{and}\qquad f\in\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{SAT}}.\]
Thus one fixed counting function must be strong enough to decide SAT, yet every value of that function must be computable using only polynomial time and SAT queries. Equality implies the second requirement because querying a particular output bit of \(f\) is a decision problem in \(\mathrm P^f\), and there are polynomially many bits. The converse follows by replacing oracle calls by the stated simulations. This equivalence fixes the decision/function distinction; it adds no single-query, nonadaptive or parsimonious-reduction requirement.

The existential quantifier is over all \(\#\mathrm P\) functions. The selected function need not be \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete or count satisfying assignments of its input formula. There is no requirement that one algorithm uniformly discover a suitable function from an arbitrary verifier. A refutation must rule out every possible fixed \(\#\mathrm P\) function, not just the familiar \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) function.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. A positive answer must define one total \(f\), prove its \(\#\mathrm P\) representation and prove both class containments, with the uniform polynomial-time oracle simulations justified. Equivalently, prove both concrete requirements in the definitions. A negative answer must prove that every \(f\in\#\mathrm P\) fails at least one containment. An oracle-relative separation, a conditional statement assuming an unproved class separation, an approximate count, or one candidate that fails does not settle this unrelativized question. The target is exact class equality; numerical approximation tolerances do not apply.

source_formulation.text: Conjecture 6.3 asks whether a #P function can have exactly the polynomial-time oracle power of NP.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Conjecture 6.3; the surrounding section also asks a separate oracle-construction question

context_blocks.text: A SAT oracle reports whether a witness exists. A counting oracle can disclose far more information by reporting how many witnesses exist. This question asks whether some genuine count has exactly the power of repeated SAT decisions, with neither a deficit nor a surplus of computational power.

The familiar choice \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\) counts all satisfying assignments. Toda’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{PH}\subseteq\mathrm P^{\#\mathrm{SAT}}\), where \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}\), \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\), and \(\Sigma_{i+1}^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_i^{\mathrm P}}\). Therefore equality with \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\) for this particular complete counting function would collapse the whole polynomial hierarchy to \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\). This is a conditional consequence, not a proof that this candidate or every other candidate fails.

Fortnow places the question next to the checkability of SAT: whether a randomized polynomial-time checker can assess the answer of a purported SAT solver using that solver as an oracle. The source describes a possible connection between counting and checking, not a proved equivalence between the two open questions.

The 2021 source does not even know a counting function satisfying the weaker pair \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm P^f\subseteq\mathrm{PH}\). That observation is dated context; the benchmark retains the stronger equality of Conjecture 6.3.

The surrounding article studies relativization: what happens when machines receive an additional fixed oracle. Its section heading requests an oracle world with no such counting characterization. That separate construction would not refute the ordinary-world target stated here.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), the constant-zero counting function already meets the equality. Consequently, a negative answer here would imply \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). This is an immediate consequence of the definitions, not an additional hypothesis in the card.

cards.title: Improving the log-space SAT time exponent beyond 2 cos(π/7)
cards.formal:
Let \(\alpha=2\cos(\pi/7)\), approximately \(1.8019377\). Does there exist a rational constant \(q>\alpha\) such that no uniform deterministic random-access algorithm decides SAT using both \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) workspace on every input of bit length \(N\)? In symbols, is
\[\exists q\in\mathbb Q,\quad q>2\cos(\pi/7)\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathrm{SAT}\notin\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]?\]
This is the fixed positive improvement explicitly proposed in Problem 1. The two resource bounds must belong to the same machine.
cards.why: A fixed improvement would cross a precisely understood limit of the established proof framework for unconditional SAT time-space lower bounds. It would strengthen our understanding of how little memory constrains computation on an NP-complete problem.
cards.status_note: Source-open. The full 2016 column gives this concrete target. The 2007 full manuscript’s Theorem 1.2 supports the 2008 SAT threshold, the 2015 introduction/Theorem 1.1 specify the restricted proof-rule barrier, the 2021 main statements concern distinct verification classes, and the 2023 Remark 47 still records the classical simultaneous threshold. Bounded searches through 16 September 2026 found no fixed improvement matching the stated logarithmic-space SAT target. Source/model and theorem scopes were checked; no independent proof certification of the complete lower-bound literature is claimed.

Buss and Williams establish that the formalized alternation-trading rules R0–R2 cannot improve the threshold.
Problem 1 asks for a fixed positive improvement for logarithmic workspace.
A broader lower-bound framework recovers the classical SAT exponent while giving stronger bounds for different quantum and randomized verification classes.

The proposed lower bound applies to deterministic algorithms that use only logarithmic writable memory and can query any input location.
The goal is to exclude some time exponent strictly larger than 2 cos(π/7), with the same machine subject to both resource bounds.
Known lower bounds approach the threshold from below, and a theorem limits a formalized proof method at that threshold.
A refutation must provide algorithms for every larger exponent, possibly different algorithms for different exponents.

cards.definitions:
SAT is satisfiability of explicitly encoded Boolean 3-CNF formulas, as permitted by the source. Each clause contains at most three literals, each a variable or its negation; the formula is a conjunction of clauses. It is satisfiable if some Boolean assignment to its occurring variables makes it true. Empty clauses are false and the conjunction of no clauses is true. The input is a fixed self-delimiting binary list of clauses, signed variable identifiers and delimiters. Identifiers can be chosen from \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with unused names permitted. All occurrences and identifiers count in the total bit length \(N\). The encoding is explicit, and malformed strings are rejected. Size is not just the number of variables, and there is no promise of sparse occurrences or compressed access to the formula.

Fix a deterministic random-access bit-machine model: a finite Turing-machine program with a fixed number of initially blank finite-alphabet work tapes, including a tape for a binary input address. A query reads the input bit at that address in one step, returning an endmarker out of range. Constructing, changing and storing addresses uses charged ordinary bit operations. The input is read-only. Work heads use ordinary tape moves; every distinct work cell visited, including address bits, counters and blank cells crossed, counts toward space. There are no random bits, nondeterministic choices, advice, oracles, catalytic storage or unbounded-precision unit-cost operations. The machine halts with an accept/reject answer on every input.

For a fixed \(q\), membership in \(\mathrm{DTISP}[N^q,\log N]\) means that there exist one such correct machine and constants \(C,D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with
\[\text{time on }x\le D\left\lceil(N+2)^q\right\rceil,\qquad
\text{visited work cells on }x\le C\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\]
for every binary input \(x\) of length \(N\). Bounds include parsing and malformed inputs. They are worst-case bounds with no distribution on formulas. The hidden constants may depend on the machine and on \(q\), but not on the input or its length. A different slow small-space algorithm and fast large-space algorithm do not establish this simultaneous membership.

The general-purpose random-access convention prevents a lower bound caused solely by slow movement across the input. Standard logarithmic-workspace word or work-memory random-access models can be simulated in this bit model using logarithmic space and a polynomial-logarithmic time factor. Conversely, a word machine can implement its elementary bit operations. Since the target asks for some fixed exponent strictly larger than \(\alpha\), such factors can be absorbed by choosing a slightly smaller positive improvement. This convention does not ask for a sharp model-dependent boundary at the exponent \(\alpha\) itself.

The outer quantifier chooses one \(q>\alpha\); the resulting lower bound must exclude every eligible machine and all \(C,D\). Allowing an arbitrary real exponent instead of a rational one gives the same existence question, since a rational exponent can be chosen strictly between \(\alpha\) and any proposed larger exponent. The exact trigonometric constant defines the threshold; its displayed decimal is only explanatory. A negative answer would mean that for every rational \(q>\alpha\) some eligible algorithm achieves the stated time and space bounds. These algorithms may depend on \(q\); the negation does not require a single algorithm simultaneously meeting all exponents or running in \(N^{\alpha+o(1)}\) time.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential lower-bound statement. A positive answer must specify an exponent \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\) and rule out every correct, total deterministic algorithm with simultaneous \(O(N^q)\) time and \(O(\log N)\) visited workspace. A negative answer must establish the existence of an appropriate correct algorithm for every rational \(q>2\cos(\pi/7)\), with its own fixed resource constants allowed. A result only below the threshold, for a restricted algorithm or proof paradigm, for counting satisfiable assignments, or for a larger verification class does not settle this target. Neither evidence from proof search nor an unproved hardness assumption is an unconditional solution. The exponent comparison and asymptotic quantifiers must be proved exactly; the decimal approximation and a numerical tolerance cannot replace them.

source_formulation.text: Problem 1 asks to improve SAT time lower bounds on logarithmic-space machines and explicitly proposes excluding time n raised to 2 cos(π/7) plus a fixed positive constant.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source’s concrete fixed-exponent target; rational-exponent formulation is equivalent

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space algorithm may repeatedly reread the formula while retaining very little information. Repeated reading saves memory but costs time. This card asks for a larger unconditional exponent in that time cost, with logarithmic memory kept fixed.

Williams’s lower bound rules out deterministic subpolynomial-space SAT algorithms with time exponent below \(2\cos(\pi/7)\). Subpolynomial space means \(N^{o(1)}\): smaller than every fixed positive power of \(N\), and includes logarithmic space. The target here asks to move strictly above that exponent in the particular logarithmic-space regime.

Buss and Williams prove an exact limitation of a formalized family of alternation-trading arguments. Theorem 1.1 concerns their inference rules R0–R2; these rules cannot establish a contradiction beyond the threshold. This is a theorem about those proof rules, not an upper-bound algorithm for SAT or an impossibility theorem for all mathematical lower-bound arguments.

The 2021 paper obtains stronger exponents for problems admitting quantum or randomized verification with a proposed witness. It also recovers the classical SAT threshold in its general framework. The stronger results retain their different verification classes and cannot be read as an improved SAT exponent.

The 2023 discussion separates two kinds of lower bounds. A simultaneous bound excludes a single machine that is both fast and space-efficient. A separate-algorithm alternative says that SAT cannot have both a fast algorithm and another sufficiently space-efficient algorithm. The logical forms differ, and neither removes its space qualification automatically.

Proving one larger fixed exponent would be a concrete advance, but would not by itself prove P ≠ NP or L ≠ NP. A logarithmic-space SAT algorithm, if one existed, could still have a larger fixed polynomial running time. Excluding all polynomial exponents in logarithmic space would be the stronger class separation.

cards.title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm P\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(L\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.

source_formulation.text: The source asks whether its terminating two-destination ARRIVAL decision problem belongs to P, while establishing verifiable certificates for both possible destinations.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the full passage on page 69:4, with the instance model from §2

cards.why: ARRIVAL isolates the complexity of a finite deterministic process with one bit of memory at each switch. Its outcome has short verifiable evidence on both sides, but a general efficient decision algorithm would need to go beyond following the potentially exponential trajectory.
cards.status_note: Source-open. The 2021 source’s complete instance definition, termination lemmas, main runtime theorem and proof were checked. The 2025 recursive/contraction paper and the published May 2026 ladder paper explicitly retain the general polynomial-time question; their restrictions and complexity measures were checked. Bounded later-work searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution. The full later proofs have not been independently audited or formalized in Lean.

The FUN paper proves polynomial time on binary ladders and explicitly retains the general ARRIVAL-in-P question.

sentences: ARRIVAL asks which of two destinations is reached by one token following deterministic alternating switches.
The graph and both successor choices are explicit, and every vertex can reach at least one sink in the underlying graph.
The target is one deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm, without requiring it to list the token trajectory.
General subexponential algorithms and newer bounded-treewidth or ladder results leave that all-instance target open.
Short certificates for both outcomes make this a basic unresolved question at the boundary of efficient decision and total search.

cards.definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. The class \(\mathrm P\) means one uniform deterministic program deciding this language on all input strings in a worst-case polynomial number of ordinary bit operations. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm P\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.

context_blocks.text: The local rule is elementary, but a vertex remembers which of its two arcs should be used next. With n vertices there are 2ⁿ possible switch configurations in addition to the token position. Long deterministic runs therefore do not contradict the small size of the graph. Ordinary reachability ignores these switch settings and does not decide which sink the token actually reaches.

The source gives short verifiable certificates for both answers using switching flows: counts of traversals that obey conservation and alternation. This places the decision problem in NP ∩ coNP. Certificates can establish the outcome without listing an exponentially long trajectory, but their existence does not itself provide a polynomial-time way to find them.

The 2021 algorithm runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) time and becomes polynomial when deleting a fixed number of vertices makes the graph acyclic. The former is a general improvement over direct simulation; the latter keeps a structural restriction. Neither is the all-instance polynomial bound asked for here.

The 2025 work gives a bound \(2^{O(k\log^2 n)}\) for treewidth \(k\), which is quasipolynomial, not polynomial, even when \(k\) is fixed. It also relates ARRIVAL to approximate fixed points of contractions in the ℓ₁ metric. The paper explicitly distinguishes polynomially many function evaluations from a polynomial total running time.

The 2026 paper proves polynomial time for binary ladders: simple switch graphs with exactly two vertices at each occupied distance level from the two sinks. Such graphs can frustrate earlier algorithms, so solving them is meaningful progress. The restriction concerns the shortest-distance layers of the graph and is not satisfied by general instances.

A polynomial-time algorithm would settle a basic deterministic process whose YES and NO answers already have efficiently checked evidence. A lower bound excluding all such algorithms would be a major complexity separation; the difficulty of simulating the process is only one part of that question.

cards.title: Closure of UL under complement
cards.formal:
Is unambiguous logarithmic space closed under Boolean complement?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*,\qquad L\in\mathrm{UL}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{0,1\}^*\setminus L\in\mathrm{UL}.\]
Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{coUL}\)? A language is in \(\mathrm{UL}\) if one uniform nondeterministic machine decides it using logarithmic work space and has at most one accepting computation path on every input.

The complementing machine must also have at most one accepting path on every input and logarithmic space with its own fixed constants. The question concerns ordinary uniform machines with no advice or oracle and arbitrary binary input languages, not only planar graph problems.

source_formulation.text: Thus it is far less clear what it should mean to say that a function is “computable in UL” since it remains an open question […]
source_formulation.caption: Truncated source excerpt (at most 25 words); PDF p. 3

cards.why: Unambiguity retains existential computation while limiting each positive instance to a unique accepting history. Complement closure asks whether the same economy is available for negative instances. Its resolution would clarify a basic structural property between deterministic and nondeterministic logarithmic space and the interpretation and composition of functions computed using unambiguous subroutines.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: MFCS 2021 Section 2, the primary publisher statement of nondeterministic-space complementation, and the MFCS 2026 long-path abstract and metadata. A bounded later-work search found no general uniform UL-complementation proof or counterexample. The recent parameterized result and catalytic variants use different scopes or models. This source-open classification records those limitations and does not independently certify current openness.

sentences: UL contains languages decided with logarithmic work space and at most one accepting computation path per input.
The question asks whether the complement of every such language also has an unambiguous logarithmic-space decider.
The original and complement machines are uniform, exact and have no oracle or nonuniform advice.
Ordinary nondeterministic logspace is closed under complement, but its complementing procedures need not preserve unambiguity.
A resolution would clarify both the structure of small-space complexity classes and the use of unambiguous subroutines in graph algorithms.

cards.definitions:
A language is any set of finite binary strings, and \(n=|x|\) denotes input length. Use a nondeterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite control and fixed finite tape alphabets, a two-way read-only input tape with end markers, and finitely many initially blank work tapes. Each transition has at most two choices. The input cannot be modified or used as additional writable memory. Work space is the total number of work-tape cells visited along a computation, measured in bits up to the fixed alphabet factor; the input cells and fixed finite control are not charged as work space.

A machine is logarithmic-space bounded if there is a constant \(c\) such that every computation on every input of length \(n\) visits at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. Use the standard halting convention: some fixed polynomial \(K(n+2)^d\) bounds the number of steps along every computation path, including rejecting paths. The machine and \(c,K,d\) are fixed independently of the input. A polynomial clock fits in logarithmic space; this convention does not add a nonuniform resource.

A computation path is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to an accepting or rejecting halt. Distinct choice histories count as distinct paths even when they later reach the same configuration. Acceptance means that at least one path accepts. The machine decides \(L\) when it accepts exactly the strings of \(L\); all paths on strings outside \(L\) reject.

Unambiguity means at most one accepting path for every binary input. Therefore a yes-instance has exactly one accepting path, while a no-instance has none. There may be many rejecting paths in either case. No probability distribution or bounded-error interpretation of these paths is intended. This is not the stronger requirement that every configuration, or every pair of configurations, be connected by at most one path.

The class \(\mathrm{UL}\) consists of languages decided by some machine satisfying all these conditions. Define \(\mathrm{coUL}=\{\overline L:L\in\mathrm{UL}\}\), where \(\overline L=\{0,1\}^*\setminus L\). Dropping only the unambiguity restriction gives \(\mathrm{NL}\), and restricting to deterministic transitions gives \(\mathrm L\). The usual inclusions are \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\). The known closure \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) makes \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{NL}\) sufficient for the requested closure; no equivalence to that stronger equality is asserted.

The quantifier is over languages: for each language with a qualifying machine, another qualifying machine for its complement must exist. An effective compiler that transforms every description of an unambiguous machine into a complement machine is not additionally required. Nor must the original and complement machines have the same space constant or polynomial clock. A negative answer is a language in \(\mathrm{UL}\) whose complement is not in \(\mathrm{UL}\), with nonmembership excluding all possible unambiguous logarithmic-space machines.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of closure in the declared uniform model. A proof must establish a qualifying complement machine for every language in UL, with exact acceptance, unambiguity on all inputs and logarithmic work space. A refutation must establish a language in UL and prove that its complement has no such machine. Merely complementing nondeterministic logspace while allowing multiple accepting paths, adding advice or an oracle, or settling a restricted family of graph inputs does not meet the full criterion. An oracle separation or a conditional separation alone is not an unconditional refutation.

context_blocks.text: The source explicitly distinguishes UL from its intersection with coUL when defining functions computed using unambiguous subroutines. Its convenient oracle, circuit and bit-graph descriptions agree for that intersection, whereas general UL complementation is still an open premise.
Nondeterministic space at least logarithmic is known to be closed under complement. The theorem permits several accepting histories, so it does not alone give an unambiguous complement machine.

The 2026 long-path paper obtains new parameterized algorithms and states separate unambiguous and co-unambiguous guarantees for one resource bound. Such results concern a specified graph task and its parameter; they do not establish closure for every UL language. Only its abstract and stated resource scope were used in this status check.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
cards.formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants \(c_{M} \ge  1\) and an integer \(d_{M} \ge  1\) so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair \((x,M(x))\), uses at most \(c_{M} S_{M}(x)\) tape cells, and takes at most \(c_{M} T_{M}(x)^{d_{M}}\) steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here \(S_{M}\) counts total storage including input and output, and \(T_{M}\) is at least the input length, as defined below.
cards.definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. \(S_{M}(x)\) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. \(T_{M}(x)\) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and \(M(x)\), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with \(O(S)\) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.

cards.title: Closure of SZK under truth-table reductions
cards.formal:
Is statistical zero knowledge closed under deterministic polynomial-time truth-table reductions, using the promise-problem and three-valued circuit semantics of the source? In symbols,
\[\forall A,B,\qquad B\in\mathrm{SZK}\ \land\ A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A\in\mathrm{SZK}.\]
The reduction writes all queries before obtaining their answers and combines those answers with an arbitrary polynomial-size Boolean circuit. Its circuit need not have logarithmic depth or be a polynomial-size formula. Queries outside the oracle’s promise are permitted under the explicit rules below.
cards.why: A positive answer would make statistical zero knowledge robust under a broad form of efficient nonadaptive composition. A negative answer would reveal a basic limitation on combining individually private verification tasks, despite the known strong formula closure.
cards.status_note: Source-open: the final ITCS 2023 paper explicitly poses the question after Theorem 20, under its Definition 19. The original JACM 2003 Definitions 4.6 and 4.12–4.13 and the formula-closure proof/Corollary 4.14 were read to recover the precise promise semantics. The accepted December 2024 manuscript of the 2025 TOCT paper was checked at §7/Definitions 7.1–7.2/Theorem 7.8 and the surrounding proof for the restricted later result. Bounded subsequent-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching general closure theorem or unconditional refutation; no exhaustive open-status certification or independent verification of every cited proof is claimed.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(A=(A_Y,A_N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^{*}\). Correctness requires acceptance on \(A_Y\) and rejection on \(A_N\); inputs outside their union have no required answer. A polynomial-time many-one reduction \(h\) from \(A\) to \(B\) is one uniform deterministic algorithm with running time at most \(C(n+1)^d\), for fixed constants \(C,d\), such that \(h(A_Y)\subseteq B_Y\) and \(h(A_N)\subseteq B_N\). Its behavior outside the promise is unrestricted. All lengths and time bounds refer to full explicit binary encodings.

For a self-contained definition of SZK, use its standard complete promise problem Statistical Difference, SD. A well-formed SD instance is a pair of explicitly described Boolean sampling circuits \(C:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) and \(D:\{0,1\}^{r}\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\). A circuit is a finite acyclic list of binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and constants, with its input and output wires explicitly listed. The integers \(m,r,\ell\) and all wire indices are part of the description; each listed input wire receives an independent fair bit. Let \(X=C(U_m)\) and \(Y=D(U_r)\), with \(U_s\) uniform on all \(s\)-bit strings. Their statistical distance is
\[\Delta(X,Y)=\frac12\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}}\bigl|\Pr[X=z]-\Pr[Y=z]\bigr|.\]
Set \(\mathrm{SD}_Y=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)>2/3\}\) and \(\mathrm{SD}_N=\{(C,D):\Delta(X,Y)<1/3\}\). Intermediate-distance pairs and malformed descriptions lie outside the promise. SZK is the class of all promise problems having a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to SD. By the completeness theorem this is the usual classical statistical-zero-knowledge class; no additional choice of a protocol definition is needed for this formulation.

For any promise problem \(B\), define its partial characteristic value by \(\chi_B(z)=1\) on \(B_Y\), \(0\) on \(B_N\), and \(*\) outside the promise. The reduction \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\) means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine maps each input \(x\) to a finite list \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\) and a Boolean circuit \(F\) with those \(k\) answer variables, satisfying
\[x\in A_Y\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=1,\]
\[x\in A_N\Longrightarrow F(\chi_B(z_1),\ldots,\chi_B(z_k))=0.\]
The number of queries, sum of their bit lengths and size of the explicitly written circuit are all polynomially bounded in \(|x|\). The generating machine does not query \(B\) while preparing them. \(F\) is an acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuit with constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate wires; its depth is limited only by its polynomial size. The query count may be zero. No randomized, adaptive or nonuniform reduction is allowed.

Evaluate \(F\) gate by gate over \(\{0,1,*\}\). NOT exchanges 0 and 1 and leaves \(*\) unchanged. AND returns 0 if either input is 0, returns 1 if both are 1, and returns \(*\) otherwise. OR returns 1 if either input is 1, returns 0 if both are 0, and returns \(*\) otherwise. Constants retain their values. These rules are part of the source’s definition, including on queries outside the promise. A required final value 0 or 1 is stable under replacing unknown inputs by bits, but the converse fails: \(u\lor\neg u\) evaluates to \(*\) at \(u=*\), although it is 1 on both Boolean assignments. Thus mere agreement on all Boolean completions is not silently substituted for the specified circuit semantics. Requiring every query to satisfy the promise would also change the stated reduction notion.

A Boolean formula is a circuit presented as a tree, with repeated subcomputations written out separately. Closure for polynomial-size formulas or logarithmic-depth circuits is the known restricted case. The target permits arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, whose compact descriptions may reuse intermediate results many times. The quantifiers range over arbitrary promise problems and every valid reduction of the stated kind; the polynomial bounds and programs may depend on the fixed problems and reduction, but not on individual inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal closure statement. A positive answer must show that every promise problem reducing in the specified way to any SZK promise problem itself reduces to SD, or give an equivalent fully justified SZK protocol. A negative answer must establish promise problems \(A,B\), prove \(B\in\mathrm{SZK}\) and \(A\le_{\mathrm{tt}}^{\mathrm P}B\), and prove \(A\notin\mathrm{SZK}\). The reduction’s treatment of unknown answers and its uniform polynomial bounds must be included. Closure only for formulas, logarithmic-depth circuits, or a special oracle problem does not prove the full claim without an equivalence proof. An oracle-relative or conditional separation does not refute this unrelativized target. All class, promise and probability thresholds are exact; numerical acceptance tolerance is irrelevant.

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge allows a verifier to be convinced of a statement without learning additional information, in the sense that the verifier’s view can be simulated with negligible statistical error. This card asks whether that property survives taking many nonadaptive questions and performing an arbitrary efficient Boolean computation on their answers.

The Statistical Difference complete problem makes the class concrete: distinguish two efficiently sampled distributions that are far apart from ones that are close. The middle range is deliberately left outside the promise. The card uses this characterization as its exact definition of SZK.

Sahai and Vadhan prove closure under polynomial-size Boolean formulas, and therefore under polynomial-size circuits of logarithmic depth. This is stronger than closure under a constant number of AND, OR and NOT operations, but still leaves general polynomial-depth circuit composition open.

The distinction is computational rather than a choice of logical connectives. Formulas must repeat each reused subcomputation, while circuits can share it. Replacing a circuit by its expanded expression tree need not preserve polynomial size.

The 2023 paper explicitly retains the general truth-table question while using the known formula closure in a characterization based on Kolmogorov complexity. That characterization does not claim general circuit closure.

The later space-bounded work proves a corresponding Boolean-formula closure for the logarithmic-space statistical-zero-knowledge class. Its Theorem 7.8 is a result about a restricted model and formula reductions; it does not establish the general circuit target here.

Handling queries outside the promise is essential: an SD oracle need not give meaningful information for distributions in the gap. The precise three-valued rules prevent such queries from being treated as reliable facts and preserve the formulation actually used by the source.

cards.title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
cards.formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
cards.why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

The source-open status does not certify an exhaustive literature search.

cards.definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. One verifier with intermediate acceptance probabilities, or an oracle separation, does not by itself refute the ordinary class equality.

context_blocks.text: Definition 16 applies the existential operator to ordinary languages. Remark 17 explains why fixing a witness in an MA verifier need not leave a BPP computation: a nonwinning witness on a yes-instance may lie inside the error gap. This does not itself prove that the language has no other suitable verifier.

The source encounters this distinction when bounding quantum hierarchies with classical witnesses. Its stronger-oracle simulations handle a different resource class; they do not establish the desired ordinary BPP predicate.

Fenner, Fortnow, Kurtz and Li construct an oracle relative to which MA is not contained even in nondeterministic polynomial time with access to a BPP oracle. Since existential BPP is contained in that latter class, the two target classes can differ relative to a common oracle. This is an obstruction to a proof valid under every oracle, not an unconditional separation.

cards.title: Effective enumeration of BPP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.

sentences: The problem asks for a computable list of randomized polynomial-time algorithms covering every language in BPP.
Each listed algorithm must have the required error gap on every input, but the list may repeat languages and omit alternative implementations.

cards.definitions:
All languages are subsets of finite binary strings. A randomized decision machine is a finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machine with read-only input, initially blank work tapes, a one-bit output and independent fair random bits. It has no oracle, advice or arbitrary real-number operations. Time counts ordinary tape operations, generation of random bits and output writing, in the worst case over random choices.

For each enumerated machine \(M_i\), there must exist positive integers \(C_i,d_i\) such that it halts with a decision bit within \(C_i(n+2)^{d_i}\) bit steps on every input of length \(n\) and every random-bit sequence. These constants may depend on \(i\), but not on the input or random choices. No common polynomial must bound the whole family. The time bounds are existential properties of the emitted programs; no computable method of finding their constants from \(i\), or proof certificate for those constants, is additionally required. An enumeration supplying explicit clocks would be a sufficient special case.

For every finite input, the runtime bound limits the number of coin tosses, so the acceptance probability is a well-defined dyadic rational from a finite probability space. Unused coin bits do not change an output. A machine has bounded error when its acceptance probability never lies strictly between \(1/3\) and \(2/3\). It then decides the unique language whose yes-instances have acceptance probability at least \(2/3\); every no-instance has acceptance probability at most \(1/3\). The gap must hold on every input, including the empty string.

The class \(\mathrm{BPP}\) consists of all languages decided by some randomized polynomial-time machine with this gap. Equivalently, \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) if some such machine satisfies \(\Pr[M(x)=\mathbf 1_L(x)]\ge2/3\) for every \(x\). The class \(\mathrm P\), used in the context, consists of languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time machines. Both classes use worst-case polynomial runtime.

Total computable means that one deterministic Turing machine, given the binary encoding of any nonnegative integer \(i\), halts and returns the finite transition-table code of \(M_i\). It may use arbitrarily large finite time and space as a function of \(i\). No finite or infinite advice sequence and no oracle are allowed. Codes use an ordinary effective finite encoding of machine states, tape symbols and transitions; standard such encodings can be effectively translated without changing the represented machine or its polynomial-time property.

Soundness requires every emitted machine to run in polynomial time and have the displayed gap on every input. Coverage requires that for each \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\), some index \(i\) satisfies \(L=L_i\) on all strings. Neither an index for a given language nor a decision procedure for whether an arbitrary program has the gap is requested. In particular, \(E\) may omit a bounded-error program if it lists another program deciding the same language.

The negative answer excludes every total computable enumeration with these two properties. An inability to enumerate all codes of polynomial-time bounded-error programs is a different assertion: the target only needs an effectively chosen representative family that covers all the languages. No specific logical theory or proof system is prescribed for that family.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such an enumeration. A positive answer must specify a total computable enumerator and prove the polynomial-time and all-input error guarantees for every emitted machine, as well as coverage of every BPP language. The mathematical runtime proof may establish separately quantified constants for each index without providing an algorithm computing them. A negative answer must rule out every such representative-family enumeration, including families whose time bounds are not supplied effectively. Showing that the set of all valid machine codes is undecidable or not computably enumerable does not suffice. An enumeration covering only the languages whose correctness is proved in one selected theory also does not suffice without proving that it covers all of BPP.

context_blocks.text: Section 2 emphasizes the difference between listing all algorithms with a property and listing enough algorithms to cover the same languages. The former code sets can be recursion-theoretically difficult even for deterministic polynomial time, while the latter can have a simple effective enumeration.

The source gives characterizations of BPP in arithmetic and effectively enumerable subclasses based on error guarantees provable in a sound recursively enumerable theory. Its conclusion does not show that one such subclass contains every BPP language.

Proposition 20 shows that P equal to BPP would imply the desired kind of effective characterization. Thus a proof that no covering enumeration exists would in particular separate P from BPP. The reverse implication is not asserted.

The paper proves hardness of recognizing its all-input error condition and gives an enumerable sound-theory subclass containing polynomial identity testing. These results expose the certification issue and supply substantial examples, but neither code-recognition hardness nor one such subclass settles complete language coverage.

cards.title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
cards.formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[S(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad L(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(S\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(S(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N:\quad L(f_n)>n^k.\]
This is the source's absence-of-any-polynomial-upper-bound claim. It does not silently strengthen that claim to a lower bound beating each polynomial at every sufficiently large length.
cards.why: Circuits can reuse intermediate values and formulas must duplicate the computation when it is needed again. This question asks whether reuse can turn a task requiring superpolynomial tree size into a circuit of only linear size. It isolates a fundamental limitation of formulas while allowing the circuit computation to have unrestricted depth.
cards.status_note: Conjecture 5.11 and the source’s size definitions were checked on 2026-09-14, together with Filmus–Meir–Tal’s published Theorem 1.1 and introductory status discussion and Chukhin–Kulikov–Mihajlin’s STACS 2025 introduction. A bounded search through this date found no matching superpolynomial formula separation for a linear-size circuit family or a contrary universal simulation. The source-open status has these literature-check limits; the cited proofs have not been independently formalized.

sentences: The conjecture asks for Boolean functions with linear-size circuits but no polynomial-size formulas.
Circuits may reuse intermediate results, while formulas have a tree structure and count repeated variable occurrences separately.
The computational basis is binary AND and OR with unary negation, and correctness is exact on every input.
