Known nearly cubic gaps and recent composition results do not yet give the required superpolynomial separation.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input nodes for \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and one designated output. Every computational gate is binary AND, binary OR, or unary NOT. Inputs may also supply the constant bits zero and one. Each node carries one bit, which is evaluated by applying its assigned operation to the incoming values. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and a gate value can be reused several times. The output can be an input, a constant or a computed gate. Size is the number of computational gates; input and constant nodes and wires are not charged. The circuit must output \(f_n(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). No parity or arbitrary truth-table gate is a primitive, and no random or promise-only correctness is allowed. \(S(f_n)\) is the minimum such size.

A formula is a finite rooted tree with binary AND/OR or unary NOT internal nodes and input-variable or constant leaves. Each occurrence of an input in this tree is separate; an internal computation cannot feed two parent nodes. The size of a formula is the number of variable-leaf occurrences, as in the source. Constant leaves are free; an optimum for a nonconstant function can eliminate constant subformulas. One may equivalently place all NOT operations directly on variables by De Morgan's laws, leaving the leaf count unchanged. Negated and unnegated occurrences of the same variable are each counted. \(L(f_n)\) is the minimum leaf count over formulas computing the function exactly. Constant functions have \(L=0\), and a literal has \(L=1\).

The sequence of functions, and the optimal circuits and formulas at different lengths, need not have an efficiently computable description. In particular this card does not impose an extra polynomial-time evaluator or uniform circuit-generation algorithm on the family. The source's conjecture is stated using its nonuniform size measures. A family with such extra uniformity would also qualify if it has the required sizes.

The same constant \(C\) bounds circuit size at every length. Allowing finitely many exceptions would be equivalent, since increasing \(C\) absorbs them. The formula condition is equivalent to saying that there do not exist constants \(D>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and onset \(N\) with \(L(f_n)\le Dn^k\) for all \(n\ge N\). Thus arbitrarily large violating lengths may depend on the polynomial exponent; the family itself may not. The target asserts no particular exponential or quasipolynomial lower-bound rate.

The two minima compare computations of the same single-output function. Linear circuit size does not bound circuit depth by a logarithm. A size separation using unbounded-fan-in threshold gates, only monotone formulas, or a growing number of outputs is a different statement.

The existence claim is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\subsetneq\mathrm{P/poly}\) for nonuniform Boolean circuit families. Here \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) means \(S(f_n)\le a(n+1)^b\) for some fixed positive integers \(a,b\), and \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) means a family of binary De Morgan circuits of depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for one constant \(d\); such circuits can be taken polynomial in size. No uniform generation is required in either class. Polynomial-size formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits are equivalent by formula balancing and expansion of a bounded-depth circuit into a tree.

The restriction to linear circuit size does not change this family-existence question. A separating polynomial-size family can be regarded, at lengths \(N_n=a(n+1)^b\), as a function of \(N_n\) variables that ignores the extra variables; at other lengths set the function to a constant. The circuit bound becomes linear, whereas a polynomial formula bound in \(N_n\) would give a polynomial formula bound in \(n\). This is a comparison of nonuniform families and retains the arbitrarily-large-length quantifiers. Conversely, a linear-size family is already in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). Thus an answer to the equality question has the opposite Boolean polarity from the separation question in this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed family-existence claim. A positive answer must specify or mathematically establish the existence of one family satisfying both the single linear circuit bound and failure of every polynomial formula bound. A nonconstructive family can qualify; no efficient generator is part of the target. A negative answer must show that every family with a uniform linear circuit-size constant has some polynomial formula-size bound, whose exponent and coefficient may depend on that family. Proving only one fixed polynomial separation, even with a large exponent, or refuting one candidate family does not settle the question.

The source connects its conjecture to questions about formula size under block composition. The related KRW card records a particular formula-size composition statement. This connection is contextual; the present target is stated directly in terms of the two computational size measures.

cards.title: Subexponential derandomization with two-way random-tape access
cards.formal:
Can every bounded-error randomized logspace decision algorithm with two-way access to polynomially many random bits be simulated by a deterministic algorithm in time \(2^{o(n)}\)?

Precisely, does every language \(L\in\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) admit one deterministic decider \(D\) whose worst-case running time \(T_D(n)\) satisfies
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2(T_D(n)+2)}{n}=0?\]
There is no additional space restriction on \(D\). This card uses the single-decider \(2^{o(n)}\) meaning of subexponential time, matching the explicit time scale discussed in the source. The source question is about arbitrary two-way random-tape access, even though the paper’s main advice theorem concerns a bounded number of one-way passes.

sentences: This question concerns randomized logspace algorithms that can reread a fixed polynomial-length random tape in either direction.
It asks whether every language they decide has a uniform exact deterministic algorithm whose worst-case runtime has an exponent sublinear in input length.

cards.definitions:
Inputs are finite binary strings \(x\), with length \(n\). A randomized machine is a uniform finite-program multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, a read-only random tape and a fixed number of work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input and random heads may each move one cell left or right, or stay in place, at a step; their boundaries are marked and cannot be crossed. The input may be reread without restriction.

For fixed positive integers \(a,b,c,d\) depending only on the machine, the random tape holds
\[r(n)=a(n+1)^b\]
bits sampled uniformly and independently at the start of the run, and the total work-tape storage is at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits on every input and every random string. Padding the random tape by unused random bits is allowed. A reread of a random cell returns its original sampled bit; it does not toss a new coin. The read-only input and random tapes do not count as writable work space. Any work-tape storage used for counters, remembered bits or bookkeeping does count. There is no additional stream of fresh randomness, writable uncharged auxiliary tape, advice or external oracle.

The machine halts with a one-bit accept/reject answer within \(d(n+1)^d\) steps for every random tape. This is a worst-case polynomial clock, not an expected-time convention. Polynomial time also bounds the number of changes of direction or complete passes. Head movements, tape operations and reading a random bit each cost a machine step. The algorithm may inspect random positions adaptively; no bound by a fixed number of sweeps is imposed.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{2\text{-}wayBPL}\) if some such machine \(M\) satisfies
\[\forall x\in L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall x\notin L,\quad\Pr_{r\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{0,1\}^{r(|x|)})}[M(x;r)=1]\le1/3.\]
The random-string variable in these displays is a full tape content. Correctness is required for every input separately, and all binary strings are either yes- or no-instances; there is no promise gap in the input domain. The newer notation \(\mathrm{BP}\!\cdot\!\mathrm L\) in the cited 2024 paper refers to this persistent, rereadable randomness model for decision languages. Ordinary BPL instead restricts the random tape to one-way access.

The deterministic simulator is a uniform multitape Turing decider with no random tape, advice or oracle. It must output \(1\) exactly on \(L\) and halt on every binary input. Set
\[T_D(n)=\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\operatorname{time}_D(x).\]
The required limit is equivalently: for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(N_\varepsilon\) such that \(T_D(n)\le2^{\varepsilon n}\) for all \(n\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same \(D\) must satisfy all these bounds. It may depend on \(L\), as may the thresholds; the assertion does not require an effective compiler from descriptions of randomized machines.

The criterion is not merely a running time \(2^{n^k}\) for some fixed \(k\), nor a fixed exponential saving \(2^{0.99n}\). It also does not demand the stronger family of bounds \(2^{n^\varepsilon}\) for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The selected convention is explicitly the limit above. A refutation is a language in the stated randomized class for which every correct deterministic decider fails that limit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the containment under the specified tape and runtime conventions. A proof must establish one exact deterministic decider of sublinear-exponent worst-case time for every language in the class. It need not preserve the logarithmic space bound or effectively transform arbitrary randomized machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some language in the class has no deterministic decider meeting the displayed limit. A simulation with advice, a bound only for restricted random-tape movements, correctness on most inputs or a conditional hardness-to-randomness implication alone is insufficient.

cards.title: Doubly efficient \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: For every uniform deterministic polynomial-space decider \(M\) and every time-constructible bound \(T(n)\ge n+2\) on its running time, does the language \(L(M)\) have a uniform classical single-prover interactive proof with a verifier running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time and an honest prover running in \(\operatorname{poly}(T(n))\) total time, with completeness at least \(2/3\) and soundness at most \(1/3\) against every cheating prover? The quantifier covers the full time range, rather than only \(T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}\).
cards.why: The class equality IP = PSPACE says that polynomial space can be verified efficiently, but does not by itself control the cost of generating the proof relative to the original computation. The target asks whether that prover overhead can always be polynomial while retaining soundness against an unlimited adversary.

A separate report constructs bounded-space interactive arguments from one-way functions. Its abstract explicitly limits soundness to cheating provers of bounded circuit size.

The two running-time requirements concern the honest participants. Restricting honest proof generation does not restrict cheating strategies. This distinguishes the question from argument systems whose soundness relies on an adversary’s computational limitations.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal protocol-existence assertion with all stated uniformity, total worst-case running-time, completeness and soundness requirements, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. A result covering only a restricted time range, an efficient verifier with no honest-prover bound, or computational soundness under a cryptographic assumption does not settle the assertion. The time bounds are asymptotic resource requirements, not numerical quantities with \(1/100\) additive tolerance.
cards.definitions:
Fix the standard bit-cost model of deterministic multitape Turing machines with a read-only binary input tape. A decider halts and accepts or rejects on every binary input. For each fixed \(M\), there is a polynomial \(q\) such that on every input \(x\) of length \(n\), \(M\) uses at most \(q(n+2)\) work-tape cells and takes at most \(T(n)\) steps. The same machine must satisfy both bounds. Here \(T:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\) is time-constructible in the following convention: some fixed deterministic machine, on unary input \(1^n\), outputs the binary representation of \(T(n)\) within \(K T(n)\) steps for a constant \(K\). The requirement \(T(n)\ge n+2\) merely absorbs bounded lengths. Define \(L(M)=\{x:M\text{ accepts }x\}\).

An interactive proof consists of two fixed finite programs, an honest prover \(P\) and a verifier \(V\), which both receive only the common input \(x\) and exchange finite binary messages. They may use independent private fair random bits. A protocol may expose verifier randomness through its messages, but public coins and perfect completeness are not extra requirements. The machines know their fixed protocol and may incorporate the fixed descriptions of \(M\) and a constructor for \(T\). They receive no advice depending on input length, trusted preprocessing, shared secret, additional witness, oracle, or separately supplied value of \(T(n)\).

For each fixed \(M,T\), there must be constants \(C,a,b\ge1\) and one such pair \(P,V\), all independent of \(n,x\), satisfying these bounds for every input. The verifier's total number of bit operations is at most \(C(n+2)^a\), on every random tape and against every possible sequence of prover messages. It accepts or rejects within that bound. The total number of messages, all transmitted or read message bits and verifier random bits are charged to this bound; malformed or oversized messages may be rejected. The honest prover's total number of bit operations during an interaction with \(V\) is at most \(C(T(n)+2)^b\), on every choice of both random tapes, including inputs outside the language. All input-dependent preprocessing, message generation and communication are included. No separate restriction to polynomial prover space is imposed.

Completeness requires
\[
\Pr[\langle P,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3
\quad\text{for every }x\in L(M),
\]
where the probability is over both machines' independent random bits. Soundness requires, for every \(x\notin L(M)\) and every cheating strategy \(P^*\),
\[
\Pr[\langle P^*,V\rangle(x)\text{ accepts}]\le1/3.
\]
A cheating strategy can depend arbitrarily on \(x\) and its visible transcript and can perform unlimited computation; it has no access to unexposed verifier randomness. It may be randomized, with its private randomness independent of the verifier's. There is only one prover, and no computational assumption restricts soundness.

The quantifier order is: for every fixed pair \(M,T\) satisfying the time and polynomial-space premises, there exist \(P,V,C,a,b\) that work for all inputs and lengths. No algorithm transforming descriptions of \(M,T\) into protocols is additionally demanded. The prover bound refers to the specified \(T(n)\), not to an unrestricted exponential in the space bound. The verifier bound remains polynomial in the original input length even when \(T\) is superquasipolynomial.

cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: Put \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). For \(0\le p<1/2\), let \(\mathcal C_p(n)\) be the finite noisy circuits defined below. Define reliable computation at noise \(p\) by \[\operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff \exists\delta\in(0,1/2]\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}\ \exists C\in\mathcal C_p(n)\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\Pr[C(x)=f(x)]\ge1/2+\delta.\] Is the following proposition true? \[\forall p\in[0,1/2):\quad \operatorname{Reliable}(p)\iff p<\beta.\] In particular, the proposition includes impossibility at \(p=\beta\).
cards.definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with labeled input sources \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), noiseless constant sources \(0,1\), and one designated output wire. A computational gate has one or two ordered input wires and an arbitrary fixed Boolean truth table on those bits. Wires may connect a source or an earlier gate to any number of later gates; both inputs of a gate may come from the same predecessor. There are no other gates, external coins, auxiliary inputs, or oracle operations. A gate-free output is allowed to read one source directly.

For every computational gate \(v\), independently sample \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\Pr[Z_v=1]=p\). Evaluate the DAG in topological order. If the gate truth table applied to its received bits gives \(b\), its actual value is \(b\mathbin{\oplus}Z_v\), where \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. Every outgoing wire carries this same actual value. All gate failures are mutually independent and independent of the input; wire values sharing a predecessor need not be independent. Input sources and wires are perfect. All computational gates, including NOT and any output gate, have exactly the same flip probability \(p\); no noiseless output decoder is supplied.

The probability in the target is only over this finite product of gate-failure distributions, for a fixed input \(x\). The circuit and its wiring and truth tables may depend on the real parameter \(p\), the integer \(n\), and the entire function \(f\), but not on the actual input \(x\) or realized failures. The advantage \(\delta\) may depend on \(p\), but is chosen before \(n\) and \(f\). Circuit size, depth and construction time are unrestricted, and no uniform algorithm constructing the circuits is required. A formula is the special case where every computational gate has at most one outgoing wire; an input variable can still occur on multiple leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal equivalence or its logical negation, in the specified independent gate-flip model. The same positive advantage must work for every input length and every Boolean function at each fixed noise level. The boundary \(p=\beta\) is part of the claim. A theorem only for formulas, only for a restricted gate basis, or with a separate noiseless decoder does not decide this circuit proposition. A negative resolution of reliable computation must rule out all finite circuit sizes; failure of one construction is insufficient.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The task concerns whether arbitrary computation remains possible at all under local errors, even when unlimited redundancy is permitted. The target keeps a positive correctness margin independent of the function and its number of inputs. It is not a circuit-size overhead problem or an average over randomly chosen inputs.

Unger’s theorem gives the sharp formula boundary \(\beta=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\), including failure of universal reliable computation at equality, and explicitly conjectures the extension to circuits. Formulas cannot reuse an intermediate noisy gate value; circuits can, so independent gate failures do not make the received signals independent. The positive formula result below \(\beta\) also provides circuits.

The later formulation of reliable computation in Definition 2.1 of Shutty, Wootters and Hayden uses one advantage for all Boolean functions, as here. Their survey distinguishes the symmetric two-input formula threshold from the known general-circuit upper bound \(1/2-1/(2\sqrt{2})\). Their main asymmetric model permits gate-dependent errors, including noiseless XOR, and its proposed circuit extension is conditional. Those statements do not settle the identical-noise circuit claim.

The July 2025 essay revisits established circuit-noise bounds and discusses majority gates of higher arity. Its stated scope does not supply the missing exact threshold for arbitrary two-input circuits.

cards.title: Polynomial-size closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal:
Do constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set \(X\) and every d-DNNF circuit \(C\) over \(X\), there is a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over \(X\) with
\[s(D)\le c\bigl(s(C)+1\bigr)^k\quad\text{and}\quad\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\ f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The constants are universal: they cannot depend on \(X\), \(C\) or its Boolean function. No algorithm, uniformity or bound on the time needed to find \(D\) is required. Its internal decompositions may differ from those of \(C\), with no global variable-tree restriction on either circuit.
cards.definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

The output uses only variables of \(X\), interpreted on the same coordinates, with no auxiliary variables or existential projection. It need not mention every variable. The size counts the complete circuit rather than an implicit description or an oracle for evaluating it. The target is nonconstructive representational closure with polynomial overhead, not closure as a set of Boolean functions alone.

The exact negation of the claim is that for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some finite \(X\) and some d-DNNF \(C\) have the property that every d-DNNF \(D\) computing its complement satisfies \(s(D)>c(s(C)+1)^k\). This need not be witnessed by one fixed input circuit defeating all polynomials, or by an efficiently constructible family. A uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm would imply the size bound; the converse is not part of this statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal polynomial-size closure statement. A proof must supply universal constants and establish a complement representation satisfying the bound for every input circuit. A refutation must establish the quantified superpolynomial obstruction for general output d-DNNFs. A lower bound that only excludes structured outputs, a particular decomposition or a particular algorithm is insufficient. Computational difficulty in finding a complement alone also does not refute existence of a small complement.
cards.why: This question isolates whether Boolean negation inherently destroys the succinctness of a central tractable representation. It separates a representational obstruction from the algorithmic difficulty of discovering a representation. A negative answer would exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between compact descriptions of a set of assignments and its complement; a positive answer would establish polynomial-size robustness under negation.

importance.reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.

context_blocks.text: The source question explicitly separates efficient complementation from existence of a small complement. Every Boolean complement has some d-DNNF representation; the issue is a polynomial bound, and for the computational version a uniform algorithm achieving one.

The knowledge-compilation map treats negation as a transformation with an output representation, separately from queries such as counting satisfying assignments or comparing functions. Its d-DNNF negation entry is unresolved.

Vinall-Smeeth proves a superpolynomial complement-size lower bound when the output must remain structured, even without output determinism. The source leaves unstructured d-DNNF complementation open: removing the global variable-tree restriction changes the target of the lower bound.

The 2026 probabilistic-word paper connects complement gates in tractable circuit representations to the unresolved succinctness question for d-DNNFs. This is evidence of an additional counting-language connection, not a general complement construction or lower bound.

cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for \(x_{i}\), 1 for \(\neg x_{i}\)), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: \(\lfloor \log _{2}i\rfloor\) zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with AND and OR gates of fan-in two. Each leaf is an input bit, its negation, or a Boolean constant. Equivalently, unary NOT gates can be used anywhere and then pushed to the leaves without changing the leaf count. Internal computations cannot be shared between two parents. Its size is the number of leaf occurrences, so repeated uses of the same variable are charged separately. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in \(O(\log  n)\) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves if some constant C bounds its size by \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and \(\varepsilon\), but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family has, for every \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\), some \(n\ge N_{0}\) with more than \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) leaves. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.

context_blocks.title: Uniformity constrains the whole family
context_blocks.text: A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. cards.title: Depth-three lower bounds beyond the log-depth simulation threshold
cards.formal:
Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) such that
\[S_3(f_n)=2^{\omega(n/\log\log n)}?\]
Here explicit means membership in NP, as in the source, and \(S_3\) counts gates in the smallest unrestricted-fan-in AND/OR circuit of depth three with negations available on inputs. Both top-gate orientations are covered. To avoid undefined small-length logarithms, the precise scale in the quantifiers is \(h(n)=n/\log_2\log_2(n+4)\), which has the stated asymptotics. This is Research Problem 11.2's quantitative target; the inherited description in terms of a switching-lemma barrier did not specify its much stronger exponent.
cards.why: This is the depth-three threshold that would exclude linear-size circuits of logarithmic depth for an explicit problem. It asks for a quantitative jump beyond the square-root exponent frontier, while retaining arbitrary sharing and unrestricted bottom fan-in in the shallow circuit. It therefore connects a very restricted depth model to a longstanding lower-bound goal for more general computation.
cards.status_note: The source sections and February 2026 monotone Majority preprint introduction and Theorem 1.2, together with the March 2026 ECCC revision’s discussion and Corollary 4, were checked on 2026-09-14. Both recent sources retain the unrestricted square-root frontier and distinguish their restricted or conditional results. A bounded later-work search found no matching unconditional NP-family lower bound at the source’s stronger exponent. This is source-open under a bounded literature review, not independent certification of all cited proofs.

cards.definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), the target \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is a total Boolean function. A literal is an input \(x_i\) or its complement \(1-x_i\). The two constant bits are also permitted as leaves. A \(\Sigma_3\) circuit has a single top OR gate, middle AND gates and bottom OR gates; edges go between successive layers, and bottom gates receive literals or constants. A \(\Pi_3\) circuit interchanges AND and OR. Every gate has finite but unrestricted fan-in, fan-out is unrestricted, and sharing of bottom gates is allowed. Fan-in-one gates permit padding to three layers. Empty AND and OR evaluate to one and zero respectively. There are no other operations, internal negations, parity gates, thresholds, modular gates, or auxiliary witness inputs.

Size is the total number of AND and OR gates, including the output gate and any padding gates. Input literals, constants and edges are not charged. Let \(S_{\Sigma_3}(f_n)\) and \(S_{\Pi_3}(f_n)\) be the respective minimum sizes of circuits computing \(f_n(x)\) exactly on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\); define \(S_3(f_n)\) as their minimum. The circuit at each length may be arbitrary and nonuniform. There is no bounded-bottom-fan-in, monotonicity, canonical form beyond the stated layers, or formula/no-sharing promise. Circuit minimization measures size rather than the time to find the circuit. Gates with repeated inputs can be simplified, so forbidding parallel copies of the same edge does not change the measure.

“Explicit” follows the source's Section 1.5.1: the language \(\{x:f_{|x|}(x)=1\}\) belongs to NP. Concretely, there must be one deterministic finite-program multitape Turing verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,b\), such that
\[f_n(x)=1\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{(n+1)^a}:V(x,y)=1,\]
and \(V\) halts within \((n+|y|+1)^b+b\) steps on every pair. Padding gives this exact witness length without changing NP. All reading and bit operations are charged, and no advice or oracles are available to \(V\). Polynomial-time computable functions are allowed, but polynomial-time evaluation is not additionally required. This uniform requirement belongs to the target family, not to the circuits ruled out. A counting existence proof of hard arbitrary truth tables without such a verifier does not establish explicitness.

All logarithms are base two. For a positive scale \(h(n)\), the notation \(S(f_n)=2^{\omega(h(n))}\) in the target means that for every positive integer \(r\) there is an integer \(N_r\) such that \(S(f_n)\ge2^{r h(n)}\) for every \(n\ge N_r\). One target family and one verifier must serve all these bounds; the family cannot change with \(r\). The onset may depend on \(r\). This all-sufficiently-large-length convention is part of the displayed asymptotic target, not a mere increase of a fixed constant in an exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this NP family with the stated lower bound against both orientations. A positive answer must specify the family and its verifier, prove exact-function hardness for every sufficiently large length at every exponent multiplier, and use the stated gate-count model. A negative answer must rule out every qualifying family; it need not give one finite counterexample. A \(2^{c n/\log\log n}\) lower bound for one fixed \(c\), a \(2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}\) lower bound alone, or a theorem for only monotone, bounded-bottom-fan-in or canonical circuits does not establish this claim. A conditional lower bound qualifies only if its assumption is also proved.

context_blocks.text: Lemma 11.1 gives a simulation of linear-size logarithmic-depth binary circuits by depth-three circuits of size \(2^{O(n/\log\log n)}\). Research Problem 11.2 asks to exceed every constant at that exponent scale. The conclusion concerns the combined linear-size and logarithmic-depth resource bound, and does not by itself rule out arbitrary-depth linear-size circuits.

The same chapter separately asks to exceed the \(2^{O(\sqrt n)}\) scale in Research Problem 11.15. That weaker quantitative frontier has its own active card. A solution to the present problem would exceed it by a much larger margin.

The February 2026 paper still describes the square-root exponent barrier for general depth-three circuits. Its new optimum for Majority restricts circuits to positive literals and bottom fan-in at most three, so it does not meet the unrestricted target here.

The March 2026 report discusses the same general frontier. Its stronger exponents in Corollary 4 apply under a complexity hypothesis to a specially defined canonical circuit class; they are not unconditional bounds for all circuits allowed by this card.

cards.formal:
Does there exist an explicit family of total Boolean functions \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) for which
\[S_{\Sigma_3}(f_n)=2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}?\]
The source's explicitness convention is NP membership. The minimum \(S_{\Sigma_3}\) is taken over all OR–AND–OR circuits with unrestricted fan-in and sharing, with negations allowed on input variables, and counts every gate. The target is a superconstant improvement in the exponent over \(\sqrt n\), not merely a larger fixed coefficient. It retains Research Problem 11.15's \(\Sigma_3\) orientation; it does not silently demand a simultaneous \(\Pi_3\) lower bound for the same function.
cards.why: Depth three is the first AND/OR depth at which elementary exponential lower bounds for normal forms no longer settle the complexity landscape. Beating the square-root exponent for an explicit family would improve a basic lower-bound frontier, even without reaching the much stronger exponent needed for the logarithmic-depth simulation consequence.

cards.definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), the target \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is a total Boolean function. A literal is an input \(x_i\) or its complement \(1-x_i\). The two constant bits are also permitted as leaves. A \(\Sigma_3\) circuit has a single top OR gate, middle AND gates and bottom OR gates; edges go between successive layers, and bottom gates receive literals or constants. A \(\Pi_3\) circuit interchanges AND and OR. Every gate has finite but unrestricted fan-in, fan-out is unrestricted, and sharing of bottom gates is allowed. Fan-in-one gates permit padding to three layers. Empty AND and OR evaluate to one and zero respectively. There are no other operations, internal negations, parity gates, thresholds, modular gates, or auxiliary witness inputs.

Size is the total number of AND and OR gates, including the output gate and any padding gates. Input literals, constants and edges are not charged. Let \(S_{\Sigma_3}(f_n)\) and \(S_{\Pi_3}(f_n)\) be the respective minimum sizes of circuits computing \(f_n(x)\) exactly on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\); define \(S_3(f_n)\) as their minimum. The circuit at each length may be arbitrary and nonuniform. There is no bounded-bottom-fan-in, monotonicity, canonical form beyond the stated layers, or formula/no-sharing promise. Circuit minimization measures size rather than the time to find the circuit. Gates with repeated inputs can be simplified, so forbidding parallel copies of the same edge does not change the measure.

“Explicit” follows the source's Section 1.5.1: the language \(\{x:f_{|x|}(x)=1\}\) belongs to NP. Concretely, there must be one deterministic finite-program multitape Turing verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,b\), such that
\[f_n(x)=1\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{(n+1)^a}:V(x,y)=1,\]
and \(V\) halts within \((n+|y|+1)^b+b\) steps on every pair. Padding gives this exact witness length without changing NP. All reading and bit operations are charged, and no advice or oracles are available to \(V\). Polynomial-time computable functions are allowed, but polynomial-time evaluation is not additionally required. This uniform requirement belongs to the target family, not to the circuits ruled out. A counting existence proof of hard arbitrary truth tables without such a verifier does not establish explicitness.

All logarithms are base two. For a positive scale \(h(n)\), the notation \(S(f_n)=2^{\omega(h(n))}\) in the target means that for every positive integer \(r\) there is an integer \(N_r\) such that \(S(f_n)\ge2^{r h(n)}\) for every \(n\ge N_r\). One target family and one verifier must serve all these bounds; the family cannot change with \(r\). The onset may depend on \(r\). This all-sufficiently-large-length convention is part of the displayed asymptotic target, not a mere increase of a fixed constant in an exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence claim. A positive answer must define one NP family and its uniform verifier and establish the lower bound against every permitted \(\Sigma_3\) circuit at every sufficiently large length for each exponent multiplier. A negative answer must rule out every such family; invalidating one candidate family is insufficient. Fixed-constant improvements to \(2^{c\sqrt n}\), top-fan-in bounds with an additional fixed bottom-fan-in promise, or lower bounds restricted to positive literals, formulas, arithmetic gates or canonical representations do not alone meet this target. No unproved complexity assumption is included.

context_blocks.text: The book records explicit lower bounds of the form \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}\) and asks to improve their exponent asymptotically. The word explicit matters: much larger lower bounds for arbitrary truth tables are compatible with the question remaining unresolved.

The \(\Sigma_3\) basis is an OR of CNFs, where each CNF is an AND of clauses and each clause is an OR of literals. The introductory draft sentence calling this an OR of DNFs is a typographical error: its layer definition and the subsequent CNF discussion specify OR–AND–OR. The card follows those layers.

The February 2026 paper states that the \(2^{\omega(\sqrt n)}\) frontier remains open for explicit functions. Its Theorem 1.2 gives an exponential-in-\(n\) lower bound for Majority only within monotone circuits whose bottom fan-in is at most three. That restriction is essential to the theorem and absent here.
The March 2026 manuscript separately presents conditional stronger exponents for canonical circuits. Neither the canonical restriction nor its complexity premise is part of the present question.

cards.title: FBPP versus negligible-error FBPP
cards.formal:
Under the following relational error conventions, is
\[\mathrm{FBPP}\subseteq\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}?\]
In \(\mathrm{FBPP}\), a uniform randomized algorithm receives a precision parameter \(m\ge1\) in unary, must produce a valid answer with probability at least \(1-1/m\), and may take time polynomial in \(|x|+m\). In \(\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}\), one uniform randomized algorithm receives only \(x\), runs in time polynomial in \(|x|\), and has error smaller than every inverse polynomial for all sufficiently long inputs.

Both classes range over the same polynomially bounded binary relations. Relations may be partial and need not have decidable membership. The inclusion quantifies over every such relation; a negligible-error algorithm may depend on the relation but must be one fixed algorithm for all input lengths and all inverse-polynomial comparisons.
cards.why: For a decision problem, repeated trials concern one correct bit. A relation may instead allow many different valid answers without any procedure for recognizing them. This question tests whether adjustable inverse-error running time can always be replaced by negligible failure at one fixed polynomial cost, clarifying which error-reduction properties survive in general randomized search.
cards.status_note: Checked on 2026-09-14: ITCS 2024 Definition 1 and Section 5, with the arXiv version history reconciled. Proposition 23 establishes the opposite noninclusion; the source explicitly leaves this direction open. A bounded later-work search found no matching resolution using the same polynomially bounded, possibly undecidable relation convention. It does not establish exhaustive present openness.

sentences: The question compares two error requirements for randomized algorithms that may return any valid answer to a relation.
FBPP here allows a unary precision parameter and running time polynomial in reciprocal error.
The negligible-error class instead requires one algorithm with a fixed polynomial time bound and error eventually below every inverse polynomial.
Relations may be partial and need not have an effective test for valid answers.
The source proves noninclusion in the reverse direction, leaving this inclusion versus incomparability unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A relation is any set \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*\). Its domain is \(\operatorname{dom}(R)=\{x:\exists y\ (x,y)\in R\}\). On a domain input \(x\), any \(y\) with \((x,y)\in R\) is a valid output. On inputs outside the domain, no correctness condition is imposed. Polynomially bounded means that fixed positive integers \(a,b\) exist with
\[|y|\le a(|x|+1)^b\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in R.\]
This bound is independent of a requested precision. There is no promise that membership in \(R\), its domain, or validity of a proposed answer can be computed or efficiently verified. All these relations, not merely NP search relations or total relations, are included in the quantifier.

Use finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines with binary input, a binary output string and independent unbiased random bits. Reading and writing bits and generating each random bit count as steps. There is no oracle, nonuniform advice or arbitrary real-arithmetic primitive. Runtime bounds are worst-case bounds over every input and every random-bit sequence. Each machine must halt on every run. Success probabilities refer only to its internal random bits for a fixed input, never to an average input distribution.

Formally, \(R\in\mathrm{FBPP}\) when there are a machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that \(A\), given the self-delimited pair \((x,1^m)\), halts within \(C(|x|+m+1)^d\) steps for every binary \(x\) and integer \(m\ge1\), and
\[\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(R)\ \forall m\ge1,\quad\Pr[(x,A(x,1^m))\in R]\ge1-\frac1m.\]
Here \(1^m\) is a unary string of length \(m\), not the binary encoding of \(m\). This discrete convention gives the source's arbitrary positive-error definition by taking \(m=\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\). For \(\varepsilon\ge1\) the success requirement is vacuous. The fixed polynomial output bound is a property of valid pairs; outputs on unsuccessful runs may be any strings allowed by the machine's runtime.

Formally, \(R\in\mathrm{FBPP}_{\mathrm{negl}}\) when there are a single machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(D,e\) such that \(B(x)\) halts within \(D(|x|+1)^e\) steps on every run, and
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists N_k\ \forall x\in\operatorname{dom}(R),\quad |x|\ge N_k\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[(x,B(x))\notin R]\le(|x|+2)^{-k}.\]
The exponent \(k\) ranges over positive integers and is not an input to \(B\). The threshold \(N_k\) may depend on \(B,R,k\), but not on the particular input. The same \(B,D,e\) must satisfy all these bounds. The shift by two only avoids small-length singularities and does not alter negligibility. Equivalently, the worst error over domain inputs of each length is bounded by some negligible function of that length; no computability requirement is imposed on that bounding function. At lengths with no domain inputs the guarantee is vacuous.

The first class therefore permits increasingly costly precision requests; the second requires one polynomial running-time bound with negligible error as the input length grows. No distribution on the valid answers is prescribed in either class. Different outputs on independent runs may all be valid, so this is not the unique-answer decision setting.

An affirmative answer says that every relation meeting the first definition admits some machine meeting the second. It does not require an effective transformation from descriptions of \(A\) to descriptions of \(B\). A negative answer is a polynomially bounded relation admitting such an \(A\) but no qualifying \(B\). The reverse noninclusion is a separate, already established result in the source.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated inclusion for the full class of polynomially bounded relations. A proof must establish one negligible-error, fixed-polynomial-time algorithm for each relation in FBPP, with the displayed order of quantifiers. A refutation must exhibit a relation in FBPP and exclude every algorithm meeting the negligible-error definition. Separate algorithms or polynomial exponents for separate values of the error exponent do not establish membership in the latter class. Restricting to efficiently checkable, decidable or total relations does not prove the universal inclusion. Reproving the reverse noninclusion does not refute it.

context_blocks.text: Definition 1 deliberately permits relations without an efficient validity test. It also imposes a precision-independent polynomial bound on valid output lengths, preventing improved accuracy from being obtained by changing to longer and longer answer domains.

Section 5 proves that negligible-error FBPP is not contained in the precision-parameter version. Proposition 23 uses the broader relation convention, including noncomputable validity sets. The unresolved direction here is therefore whether the precision-parameter class is properly contained in the negligible-error class or the two are incomparable.

For comparison, the source also defines a class allowing time polynomial in input length and the logarithm of reciprocal error. That stronger runtime guarantee implies negligible-error membership. Its inclusion does not answer the question for algorithms allowed polynomial dependence on reciprocal error itself.

The source’s class separations and advice results emphasize that relational randomized computation can behave differently from BPP decision languages. This card isolates the error-convention question and includes no advice, quantum computation or prescribed sampling distribution.

cards.title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
cards.formal: For every space-constructible function \(s:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) with \(s(n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\), is every language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) decidable deterministically in \(o(s(n)^{2})\) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an \(O(s(n))\)-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace \(g_{D}(n)\) on n-bit inputs satisfies \(\lim (n\to \infty ) g_{D}(n)/s(n)^{2}=0\)?
cards.why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.
cards.status_note: Full source question read and standard space conventions made explicit. cards.definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) denotes languages with such a machine using at most \(C s(n)\) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on \(1^{n}\) can output \(1^{s}(n)\) using \(O(s(n))\) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving \(s^{2- \varepsilon}\) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of \(s(n)^{2}\). Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in \(s(n)^{2}, a\) simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.

cards.title: Deterministic query complexity of tournament kings
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\), the minimum worst-case number of edge-orientation queries needed by a deterministic decision tree to output one king of every tournament on \([n]\). The domain is the integers \(n\ge 2\). The required precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to absolute constant factors: supply a positive function \(f\) and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge 2\) such that \(c f(n)\le D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\le C f(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_0\).
cards.why: This is a longstanding total search problem in which existence is elementary but the information needed for deterministic discovery is unresolved. It isolates a substantial gap between deterministic and randomized access to a graph, without the computational cost of processing already known edges. A tight bound would explain how much pairwise information is inherently required to identify a vertex with global two-step reachability, a tournament solution motivated by pairwise competition and social choice.
cards.status_note: The FSTTCS 2025 paper explicitly leaves this deterministic gap open. The original bounds and the 2022–2024 related results were checked against primary papers. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified improvement settling the target; this is a bounded search, not an independent verification of all proofs or an exhaustive current-status certification.

progress.text: Shen, Sheng and Wu prove an \(O(n^{3/2})\) upper bound and an \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) lower bound for finding one king. Their matching \(\Theta(n^{3/2})\) result concerns a sorted sequence of kings and does not close the single-output gap.

Lachish, Reidl and Trehan obtain \(O(n^{4/3}\operatorname{polylog} n)\) queries for a vertex that reaches at least a \(1/2+2/17\) fraction of all vertices within two steps. The fraction is strictly below one.

Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh prove randomized bounds between \(\Omega(n)\) and \(O(n\log\log n)\), and quantum bounds matching up to polylogarithmic factors around \(\sqrt n\), with bounded error. These do not alter the deterministic bounds.
Abboud, Grossman, Naor and Solomon give a zero-error randomized algorithm using at most \(2n\) queries in expectation. Their Question 7 separately restates the unresolved deterministic gap.

Ismaili Alaoui and Mande prove \(\Theta(n^2)\) randomized query complexity for king existence in general digraphs and for strong-king search in tournaments. Their concluding Section 5 again identifies ordinary deterministic king search as open with the 2003 bounds.

importance.reason: A well-established query-complexity gap for a canonical total graph search problem, with a pronounced deterministic–randomized distinction and sustained independent work since 2003.

sentences: A king in a tournament reaches every other vertex along a directed path of at most two edges.
A deterministic algorithm learns the orientation of one chosen edge per query and must output a king for every tournament.
The target is its optimal worst-case query count up to constant factors as the number of vertices grows.
The checked deterministic bounds remain \(\Omega(n^{4/3})\) and \(O(n^{3/2})\), whereas randomization permits linear expected query cost.
Closing the deterministic gap would quantify how much pairwise information this total search task inherently requires.

cards.definitions: A tournament on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a loopless directed graph having exactly one of the arcs \(i\to j\) and \(j\to i\) for each distinct pair. Represent it by a bit \(x_{ij}\) for each \(1\le i<j\le n\): value 1 means \(i\to j\), and value 0 means \(j\to i\). Every assignment of these \(\binom n2\) bits is a valid input; there are no transitivity, degree or distribution promises. A vertex \(v\) is a king if for every \(u\ne v\), either \(v\to u\), or there exists \(w\in[n]\setminus\{u,v\}\) with \(v\to w\) and \(w\to u\). Thus the path must follow the arrows and have at most two edges. The task is to output any one such vertex, rather than to decide whether one exists, to verify a given candidate, or to output every king. A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node names a pair \(i<j\), its two outgoing edges are labeled 0 and 1, and each leaf names one vertex. Starting at the root, the input follows the edge matching the named input bit. The tree is correct if the leaf reached is a king for every complete bit assignment. Its cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited over all inputs. Define \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) as the minimum cost of a correct tree for that n. The tree may choose later queries from previous answers. Only single-edge queries are charged; internal computation, storage, knowledge of n and production of the vertex label are free. Separate trees may be chosen for each n; no polynomial-time construction or uniform generation of their descriptions is required. There are no random coins, quantum queries or additional graph oracles. Every nonempty tournament has a king, so this minimum is finite; the omitted one-vertex case has cost zero. Constants in the asymptotic answer are independent of n and of the tournament, and logarithmic factors are not absorbed into those constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked characterization of \(D_{\mathrm{king}}(n)\) to the stated constant-factor precision. An acceptable positive function \(f\) must be specified by an unambiguous mathematical description and accompanied by proofs of both bounds for every sufficiently large integer n in the stated decision-tree model. The upper bound must establish correct trees at all such sizes; the lower bound must apply to every correct tree. Merely renaming the defining minimum, bounding only its exponent while leaving nonconstant factors unspecified, or improving just one side of the gap does not meet this criterion. This is an asymptotic target, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not an additive tolerance on its growth rate.

context_blocks.text: Pairwise outcomes can cycle: one player defeats a second, the second defeats a third, and the third defeats the first. A king need not defeat everyone directly; it must defeat each other player either directly or through one intermediary. In that three-cycle all three vertices qualify. The task therefore allows multiple correct outputs and does not impose an ordering or tie-breaking rule.

The graph is hidden behind edge queries. Reading its entire adjacency table always supplies enough information, but a search algorithm may stop once the answers force one output vertex to be a king in every tournament consistent with them. The central question is the optimal amount of information for this search relation, with unrestricted computation on what has been learned.

The source asks to determine the deterministic complexity without proposing a particular exponent as the answer. This card makes the requested asymptotic precision explicit as \(\Theta\), preserving the full gap question. An upper bound of \(O(n^{4/3})\) or a lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) would match a known opposite bound, but neither exponent is imposed as the conjectured answer.

A zero-error randomized algorithm can have a small expected number of queries while some random outcomes use more. A bounded-error randomized algorithm instead permits a small failure probability on each fixed tournament. Both differ from the deterministic worst-case target. Similarly, reaching a fixed fraction of vertices is a weaker output requirement than being a king.

The 2025 paper resolves two nearby questions: deciding king existence in arbitrary directed graphs, and finding a strong king in a tournament. A strong king satisfies an additional comparison between numbers of two-edge paths in opposite directions. Neither result gives the optimum for finding an ordinary king in a tournament, and the paper explicitly keeps this latter question open.

cards.title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{n}\) encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each \(T_{j}\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
cards.definitions: A literal is either \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
cards.why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

progress.text: Monet formulates the binary-weight optimization problem and records NP membership of its decision version, polynomial-time weighted satisfaction, and a pseudopolynomial dynamic program for falsification.
The Dagstuhl seminar on database representation and provenance presents this exact question by linking to Monet’s formulation. The catalogue’s separate TCS-0485 record comes from that link.

Amarilli’s maintained list still asks for a polynomial-time weighted-falsifiability algorithm and discusses its connection to complementation of d-DNNFs. Monet’s original question has no posted answer at this check.

context_blocks.text: Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from \(2^{n}\) decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take \(F=(x \mathrm{AND} y) \mathrm{OR} ((\mathrm{NOT} x) \mathrm{AND} z)\), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment \((1,0,1)\) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.

cards.title: Cost of restricting linear circuits to depth two
cards.formal:
Determine the asymptotic order, up to constant factors, of each of the three depth-restriction penalties
\[D_L(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{L,2}(A)}{C_L(A)},\qquad L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}.\]
The numerator restricts a circuit to two leveled addition layers and the denominator allows arbitrary depth, with the same operation and matrix in each ratio. Size counts wires, fan-in is unrestricted, and matrices are square of dimension \(n\). This quantifies Problem 7.6 for the three linear-computation systems in the book; it does not ask only whether a gap can grow.
cards.why: Sharing through many intermediate stages can make a linear transformation substantially cheaper than a single layer of shared sums followed by outputs. These three functions quantify that saving for merging, exact addition, and parity cancellation. They isolate the role of depth without changing the operation or the target matrix.
cards.status_note: The book’s conventions and Problem 7.6 were read on 2026-09-14. The author’s update index and the full June 2017 solution note were checked; the latter explicitly establishes a polynomial XOR depth gap. Bounded subsequent searches did not locate constant-factor determinations of all three maximal penalties. The card remains source-open for this quantitative target and does not retain the obsolete claim that only polylogarithmic XOR gaps are known. The author note is identified by its publication format and date, rather than represented as a separate peer-reviewed paper.

sentences: The problem asks how much more expensive a matrix transformation can become when its circuit is restricted to two addition layers.
It compares the minimum wire count at depth two with the unrestricted minimum for the same matrix and operation.
Boolean OR, ordinary addition and addition modulo two have separate extremal penalty functions.
A 2017 result already gives a polynomial penalty for XOR, resolving a narrower earlier question.
The remaining target is the optimal asymptotic order of each penalty, with upper and lower bounds matching within constants.

cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M_n=\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}\) for integers \(n\ge1\). Rows index outputs and columns index inputs. For \(A=(a_{ij})\), the output coordinate is \(y_i=\mathop{\circ}_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\), where the operation is Boolean OR, nonnegative-integer addition (SUM), or addition modulo two (XOR). An empty sum is zero. OR and XOR inputs range over \(\{0,1\}^n\); SUM inputs range over \(\mathbb N^n\), with \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). The matrix entries only select terms; multiplication gates are not part of the model.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(n\) distinct designated input vertices of indegree zero and \(n\) distinct designated output vertices of outdegree zero, disjoint from the input vertices. Every noninput vertex sums the values of its incoming neighbors using the one chosen operation. An indegree-zero noninput vertex, in particular a zero output, computes zero. Fan-in and fan-out have no finite uniform bound, and a value may be reused at several later vertices. Graph edges carry one value and there are no parallel edges. Unary gates copy a value. Circuits compute all output coordinates exactly and simultaneously, for every input in the relevant domain. There are no negative coefficients, NOT gates, mixed operations, advice inputs, or random errors in these three addition models.

Size is the number of edges, also called wires. Every edge counts, including input edges and edges into outputs; gate count and the bit complexity of evaluating an integer sum are not the size measure. Let \(C_L(A)\) be the minimum size for \(L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}\), with depth unrestricted. This is a nonuniform minimum: the circuit can depend arbitrarily on the full matrix, and no efficient construction from its encoding is required. Matrices with nonzero entries have positive complexity. The all-zero matrix is excluded from ratios to avoid \(0/0\).

For the depth-two version \(C_{L,2}(A)\), follow the source's leveled convention: inputs, one intermediate layer, and outputs are three disjoint levels, with edges only from inputs to the intermediate layer or from that layer to outputs. Direct input-to-output edges are not allowed in this version. The intermediate layer may have any finite size; zero outputs and unary gates are allowed. Equivalently, \(C_{L,2}(A)\) minimizes \(|P|+|Q|\) over Boolean matrices \(P\in\{0,1\}^{n\times r}\), \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{r\times n}\), for any integer \(r\ge0\), satisfying \(A=PQ\) over the specified semiring, where \(|P|,|Q|\) count their one-entries. Thus in the SUM case the integer product must have exactly the prescribed zero-one entries, without duplicate contributions.

All these minima exist, and maxima over \(\mathcal M_n\) exist because the matrix set is finite. The extremizing matrices in two different ratios need not be the same. A dimensional asymptotic bound concerns \(n\to\infty\) through all positive integers, with base-two logarithms.
cards.answer_criterion: Give positive comparison functions \(d_{\mathrm{OR}},d_{\mathrm{SUM}},d_{\mathrm{XOR}}\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(D_L(n)=\Theta(d_L(n))\) for each specified operation. The constants and onset may depend on the selected operation but not on the matrix or dimension. Bounds must hold at every sufficiently large dimension, with a universal upper bound on all matrices and a matching extremal lower bound. No common extremizing matrix across the three operations is required. A proven nonconstructive existence theorem can establish an extremal lower bound. Merely improving a known lower bound, showing an unbounded or polynomial gap, or restating the circuit-minimization definition does not determine the requested orders.

context_blocks.text: The 2013 discussion gives a roughly square-root depth penalty for OR circuits and weaker explicit examples for XOR. It distinguishes the broad quantitative Problem 7.6 from Problem 7.7, which merely asks whether the XOR penalty can exceed all polylogarithmic bounds.

The author-hosted June 2017 note resolves that narrower Problem 7.7 affirmatively: it states a family of \(N\times N\) matrices with \(C_{\mathrm{XOR},2}(A)/C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)=\Omega(N^{0.3}/\log N)\). This is a polynomial separation, so the earlier polylogarithmic frontier must not be reported as current. The note does not claim to determine the maximum penalty up to constants.

Both unrestricted and depth-two complexity are nonuniform optima in this question. Efficiently finding a shallow circuit from a given deep circuit is a different algorithmic problem. Likewise, comparing OR with SUM at the same depth changes the allowed operation and belongs to the related separation card.

The source uses a leveled depth convention. The factorization definition in this card makes explicit that a direct input-to-output wire must be represented through the intermediate level, so numerical circuit-size conventions do not remain implicit.

cards.title: Nonlinear-gate advantages for binary linear operators
cards.formal:
Can arbitrary Boolean gates give an unbounded wire saving over XOR gates for computing a binary linear operator? Determine whether
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\setminus\{0\}:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A).\]
Both models allow unrestricted fan-in, fan-out and depth and must compute the entire same map \(x\mapsto Ax\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) on every input. GEN permits an arbitrary Boolean function at each gate and charges its incoming wires, not the gate's internal implementation. This adopts the unbounded-factor meaning of “help” made explicit by the constant-factor comparison following Problem 7.18.
cards.why: The final map is linear, but a general circuit may pass through nonlinear intermediate values. The question asks whether such intermediate computation can ever save an unbounded number of wires relative to staying linear throughout. It tests a basic structural limitation of circuit computation over the two-element field, where familiar linearization statements from infinite-field settings cannot simply be imported.

cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo two. For an integer \(n\ge1\), a matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) defines the total map \(x\mapsto Ax\) from \(\mathbb F_2^n\) to itself, with \((Ax)_i=\bigoplus_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\). An empty XOR is zero.

Both types of circuit are finite directed acyclic graphs with distinct input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and distinct output vertices \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), with the input and output sets disjoint. Inputs have indegree zero and outputs have outdegree zero. Intermediate nodes and output nodes compute functions of their incoming values. Fan-in and fan-out are unrestricted; every edge counts as one wire, including edges into output nodes. Unary gates are permitted. The graph has no parallel edges and there is no depth bound. Size counts wires, not gates, truth-table bits, or the time to evaluate the gates.

In the XOR model every noninput node computes the XOR of all its incoming bits, with a zero-input node computing zero. In the GEN model a noninput node of indegree \(k\) may compute any fixed Boolean function \(\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\); this includes unary negation, constants and nonlinear functions. Its input wires are ordered when specifying this function. Gate functions and wiring may depend arbitrarily on \(A\), but not on the input vector beyond the values carried by their specified wires. The gate's truth table is not charged; each value transmitted along a wire is one bit. There are no external oracles, advice inputs, random choices, or correctness promises on the input vector.

Write \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) for the respective minimum wire counts of circuits computing every coordinate of \(Ax\) exactly for every \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\). These finite minima are nonuniform circuit quantities; no efficient algorithm producing an optimum from \(A\) is required. For a nonzero matrix both minima are positive, and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\le C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) because parity is an allowed general gate. Restricting to nonzero matrices avoids undefined ratios. Arbitrary gates of unbounded fan-in are essential to the source's GEN model; replacing them with a fixed binary Boolean basis would change the question.

The positive constant \(K\) is chosen before the dimension and matrix. They may depend on \(K\), and may be obtained by a nonconstructive argument. A negative answer is exactly a finite constant \(K\) for which \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) holds for all dimensions and matrices. Computation only on the unit basis vectors is insufficient: nonlinear circuits need not be determined on other inputs by their behavior on that basis.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated unbounded-ratio assertion. A positive answer must establish arbitrarily large wire savings for some matrices, with no prescribed rate or efficient-generation requirement. A negative answer must establish a universal finite simulation factor for every square matrix. A result only for most matrices, for bounded depth, for gates with a bounded arity or fixed basis, or for correctness solely on a selected set of inputs does not settle the claim. A static data-structure lower bound must be shown to imply the exact unrestricted circuit comparison before it can serve as a resolution. No complexity conjecture is assumed.

cards.title: Largest separation between SUM and OR circuits
cards.formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the largest possible SUM-over-OR wire-complexity gaps
\[G(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM}}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A)},\qquad
G_2(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM},2}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR},2}(A)}.\]
The first ratio allows both circuits arbitrary depth; the second restricts both to the source's two-layer addition model. This retains the two comparisons explicitly motivating Problem 7.1. It compares two ways of evaluating the same zero-one coefficient matrix, not the largest SUM complexity and largest OR complexity on separately chosen matrices.
cards.why: OR can merge repeated contributions while ordinary addition must count each contribution exactly once. The largest possible size difference quantifies how much this idempotence helps when many outputs share partial computations. Separating the unrestricted and depth-two gaps tests how this advantage interacts with the number of computational layers.
cards.status_note: The source’s definitions, Problem 7.1 and Sections 5.1–5.2 were read on 2026-09-14, together with the JCSS 2016 author manuscript Sections 1–3. The author-maintained book update index was checked, and bounded searches for subsequent SUM/OR and rectifier-network separation results did not locate matching constant-factor determinations of both extrema. Publication chronology was reconciled against the paper’s statement that the book extends its earlier preprint. Source-open status records these search limits rather than a proof that no newer resolution exists.
